Kincaid played on 77% of offensive snaps (his highest since Week 9 of 2024) and ran a route on 71% of the team's passing plays (highest since Week 6 of 2024). We've seen big games from Kincaid before -- he scored 14-plus points six times last season, after all -- but the 2023 first-round pick has yet to emerge as a consistent fantasy option. Of course, if his Week 1 usage holds, he certainly can deliver TE1 fantasy numbers in Buffalo's offense. He's a fringe starting option against a Detroit defense that allowed a 7-87-2 receiving line to New Orleans tight ends last week. Over/under: 56.2 (highest) Win probability: Bills 56% (14th highest) Carolina Panthers @ Atlanta Falcons Projected score: Falcons 23, Panthers 22 Lineup locks: Bijan Robinson , Drake London , Tetairoa McMillan Fantasy scoop: Jalen Coker exploded for eight catches, 138 yards and two touchdowns on a team-high nine targets against the Bears on Sunday. Coker was Carolina's clear No. 2 target, as he and McMillan were the only Panthers to clear five targets. Coker is now firmly on the fantasy radar, but boom/bust production is likely. Of the 22 career games in which he has played over 50% of Carolina's snaps, Coker has reached 14.0 fantasy points eight times but has been held under 8.0 points 12 times. On the plus side, he has now produced 16-plus fantasy points in three straight games tracing back to last season. Consider Coker to be a fringe WR3 against Atlanta. Over/under: 44.5 (12th highest) Win probability: Falcons 54% (lowest) Minnesota Vikings @ Chicago Bears Projected score: Bears 27, Vikings 23 Lineup locks: Caleb Williams , Aaron Jones Sr ., D'Andre Swift , Justin Jefferson , Luther Burden III , Rome Odunze , Colston Loveland Fantasy scoop: The Bears scored eight offensive touchdowns in Week 1, yet Burden (9.5 points), Odunze (7.2) and Loveland (0.0) were all fantasy disappointments. Do not fret! Loveland (team-high 25 routes), Burden (second with 21) and Odunze (fourth with 18), who was limited early after being questionable to play, remained the core of the passing game -- and that will translate to production in future weeks. Kalif Raymond was the star of the passing game (8-84-0 on nine targets) but does not make for a particularly appealing waiver add. The 32-year-old receiver is a career depth player who has yet to finish any season with more than 652 scrimmage yards -- he's been held under 300 in both of the last two seasons. Raymond will hit for the occasional big play here or there, but he's too far down the totem pole in Chicago when everyone is healthy. Expect Raymond, who has 10 touchdowns in as many seasons, to disappear from the fantasy radar in short order. Quinn Rooney/Getty Images Mackenzie Kraemer Close Works at ESPN Stats & Information Follow on X Multiple Authors Sep 17, 2026, 09:00 AM ET Email Print Open Extended Reactions Welcome to 2026 ESPN NFL Survivor ! The rules are simple: Pick one NFL team each week to win its game. If that team wins (or ties), you advance to the next week. If that team loses, you are out. Survive all 18 weeks and you can take home a share of the $25,000 grand prize. The catch is that each team can be chosen only once. While the rules are simple, the game theory is not. Depending on the size of your group or what platform you play on, the optimal selections could change drastically. Smaller groups will likely end well before Week 18, so optimizing win probability each week is paramount. However, the larger the group, the more you need to focus on saving strong teams for later, as your season is more likely to last all 18 weeks. ESPN's game requires just one team each week, so that will be the strategic focus of this column. Last week, the most-selected team on ESPN Survivor was the Los Angeles Chargers . Its upset loss to the Arizona Cardinals knocked out 21% of the field and served as the biggest Week 1 betting upset since the Tampa Bay Buccaneers stunned the New Orleans Saints in 2018. Outside of the Chargers, virtually all the other popular selections won, including this column's top choice, the Jacksonville Jaguars , who dominated the Cleveland Browns 34-10. This week, seven teams are favored by at least 6.5 points, the most in any September week since 2021. Public opinion is consolidating among two teams: the San Francisco 49ers and the Buccaneers. The 49ers are the biggest favorites, laying 13.5 at home against the Miami Dolphins . That is the largest point spread this early in the season since 2021. For contests where you only need to select one team each week, I would suggest burning the 49ers now. The win equity offered by the 49ers is unmatched by other teams this week. Recently, we've seen smaller favorites struggle early in the year. Over the last five seasons, teams favored by 6 to 9.5 points have won just 60% of the time in September compared to 78% of the time in later months. Meanwhile, double-digit favorites are 11-1 in September in that span. However, that doesn't mean there aren't other strong plays. The Buccaneers have their easiest game all season with limited future value. The Chargers project to be underselected compared to how large a favorite they are, and they are also running out of usable weeks. The Philadelphia Eagles , Kansas City Chiefs and Baltimore Ravens also make some sense as contrarian plays. My estimated exposure for multiple contests is 50% 49ers, 25% Eagles, 20% Buccaneers, and 5% Chargers. Make sure to monitor the injury report for the Raiders and Chargers, as there are several key injuries on both sides that could affect that line, which could have me pivot to the Chiefs. Note: Odds by DraftKings and subject to change. Future value based on Mike Clay's cheat sheet . 1. San Francisco 49ers (vs. Miami Dolphins ) This is the most lopsided matchup on paper all season according to ESPN Analytics, so it's hard to pass up on the "free square" in single-pick contests. The trickier decision will be handling the 49ers in bigger contests. On Splash Sports' flagship contests, saving the 49ers for Week 9 on a double-pick week against the Raiders is very valuable, though they have difficult matchups in Weeks 12-16. That said, they do not play on a holiday slate, adding to their appeal in Circa. Chance to win: 92% (ESPN Analytics), 95% (Mike Clay) Spread: 49ers -13.5 (-950 moneyline) Future value: 10th (60% average win probability) ESPN Selection: 23% 2. Philadelphia Eagles (at Tennessee Titans ) The Eagles are coming in a little under the radar this week despite facing the team with the worst record in the NFL over the past three seasons. Yes, it's a road game, but the Eagles are 30-13 on the road under Nick Sirianni, the best record in the NFL. The Titans looked miserable in Week 1, getting outgained by 172 yards against the Jets, and now they face a much tougher opponent in the Eagles. This is the easiest Eagles game all season according to ESPN Analytics and second-easiest according to Mike Clay, so while they have future value, I don't feel obligated to save them like the Ravens. However, in the Circa contest, I would downgrade the Eagles significantly as they play on both holiday slates. Chance to win: 69% (ESPN Analytics), 80% (Mike Clay) Spread: Eagles -7 (-310 moneyline) Future value: Seventh (62% average win probability) ESPN Selection: 12% 3. Tampa Bay Buccaneers (vs. Cleveland Browns ) The Buccaneers are the second-biggest favorites, and this is their largest favorite role all season on paper. For those who like to save the best teams for later, the Buccaneers are the easiest choice against the second-worst team in the NFL per ESPN Analytics. However, they are also shaping up to be very popular, which is scary for a team that has failed to cover a spread in 10 straight games dating back to last season. The Buccaneers will certainly be in my Survivor portfolio, but if selection keeps trending high, I plan to be slightly underweight. Chance to win: 79% (ESPN Analytics), 82% (Mike Clay) Spread: Buccaneers -8.5 (-410 moneyline) Future value: 19th (52% average win probability) ESPN Selection: 27% 4. Los Angeles Chargers (vs. Las Vegas Raiders ) play 1:38 Dopp lays out fantasy concerns for Justin Herbert As disappointing as the Chargers were in Week 1, that loss arguably makes them a more appealing pick in Week 2, especially in more casual pools. ESPN Analytics downgraded them from 6th to 15th in its power rankings, meaning the Chargers do not have much future value. The Raiders looked good last week against the Dolphins, but this is a much more difficult spot against the Chargers off a loss. Historically, 0-1 teams that are similar-sized favorites against 1-0 team have been great outright bets. Just monitor injuries to Ladd McConkey and Brock Bowers as both are pivotal players to each team's offense. Downgrade the Chargers in Splash Sports, as two of their easiest remaining games happen in Weeks 14 and 16. Chance to win: 69% (ESPN Analytics), 81% (Mike Clay) Spread: Chargers -6.5 (-298 moneyline) Future value: 23rd (49% average win probability) ESPN Selection: 3% 5. Kansas City Chiefs (vs. Indianapolis Colts ) If I have a large number of entries, I would consider the Chiefs instead of the Ravens for a small sprinkle. The Ravens are trending to be more than twice as popular of a pick, and the Ravens have the highest average win probability for the rest of the season according to Mike Clay's model. The Chiefs are an especially sneaky pick in the Splash Sports contest, as one of their toughest stretches all season happens from Weeks 12-16, all double-pick weeks. He analyzes football on and off the field like no one else on the planet, writing about in-season X's and O's, offseason transactions and so much more. He is the host of the Bill Barnwell Show podcast , with episodes released weekly. Barnwell joined ESPN in 2011 as a staff writer at Grantland. Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions A trend that had been a popular topic of conversation over the summer in buildings around the NFL was even more prevalent in Week 1 than I would have expected. During the offseason, organizations that have a track record of operating out of the shotgun or pistol with mobile quarterbacks made plans to move that QB under center. The Commanders, Eagles and Ravens hired new offensive coordinators in David Blough, Sean Mannion and Declan Doyle, respectively, who come from offensive trees built around under-center play. And the Vikings signed Kyler Murray , who had spent the vast majority of his college and pro careers working in the shotgun, and spent training camp working on his ability to read the field, take drops and throw from under center. Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show' Some of these organizations committed more aggressively than others in Week 1, and in the Vikings' case, the plans were thrown off by a first-quarter concussion to Murray. On a leaguewide basis, though, teams took snaps from under center at the highest rate since 2012. Why are NFL teams shifting back toward getting under center? Who benefited the most in Week 1? And will this trend stick? Coaches will talk about their philosophies during the offseason, but now that offenses had to show their cards in Week 1, the move under center is one of the more dramatic changes we've seen from NFL offenses in years. Let's cover how we got here and what might be next. Jump to: How did we get here? Why the return to under center? What's missing from the approach? Which teams have leaned in? What's next for this trend? The path to shotgun (and back) Let's go back to 2007 and the 16-0 Patriots, who produced one of the best offenses in league history with a spread attack that looked little like the league's other 31 attacks. Though the NFL had seen the "run and shoot" and K-Gun in the 1990s, those were perceived to be short-lived fads from a relatively small number of coaches. But in '07, more than 74% of Tom Brady's dropbacks came from the shotgun, a figure that was nearly double the league average. The Patriots ran more than 49% of their snaps out of shotgun, a figure that would have been even higher if they hadn't been blowing teams out in the second half and running out the clock for most of the season. Consider that in 2001, Brady's first year as a starting quarterback, the Patriots had been in the shotgun just under 14% of the time. The league as a whole was still primarily operating from under center in 2007. Even as the Patriots tore up the NFL, the other 31 offenses were in shotgun only about 26% of the time. Getting out from under center was more of a move for obvious passing situations like third-and-long or as part of a two-minute drill. On first-and-10 in 2007, NFL offenses were in shotgun only 15% of the time. The Patriots were there on 40% of their snaps. Within five years, the league had shifted. During the 2012 season, NFL teams were under center just 54% of the time, down from 74% in 2007. And in 2013, the pendulum really swung. NFL teams took more snaps out of the shotgun or pistol (which had gained a foothold in the league after traveling with Colin Kaepernick from Nevada to San Francisco and being installed by Mike Shanahan and his staff of future head coaches in Washington for Robert Griffin ) than they did from under center. That disparity continued to rise in the years to come, with both scoring and offensive efficiency gradually rising alongside. By 2023, the shotgun craze peaked. Teams ran 71% of their offensive snaps from the shotgun or pistol and just 29% from under center, nearly one-third of where it had been in 2007. At the same time, though, offensive efficiency had cratered. Teams were scoring just under 22 points per game, down three points from the high-water mark of 2020. Vic Fangio-style defenses were spreading around the league, squeezing big plays away from offenses and daring them to run the ball. Teams grew more experienced dealing with some of the problems those three- and four-wideout sets presented. And as a result, in the past few years, we've seen a shift back toward the football of years past. We've watched offenses lean into bigger personnel groupings with multiple tight ends and/or a fullback on the field, something I wrote about during the offseason in my piece on the Rams and their surprising shift to 13 personnel in the middle of the 2025 season. In part, that's to push defenses out of nickel alignments and back to their base defense with four defensive backs, which would allow offenses to get back to tormenting linebackers with the passing game. The Seahawks exploited those base defense looks during last season's run to the Super Bowl, and perhaps as a result, defenses were more aggressive about staying in their nickel defense against 12 and 13 personnel looks in Week 1 of the 2026 season. We've also seen the league get under center more often. After a decade of heading toward the shotgun, the under-center rate took a small step forward from 29% in 2023 to 30.5% in 2024. In 2025, that rate rose more dramatically to 35%. And in Week 1 of 2026, NFL offenses were under center 42.5% of the time . We're suddenly back where we were in 2013 (42.2%) in terms of under-center rate. And as you might have noticed, that decision came with plenty of scoring. Teams averaged 24.7 points per game in Week 1, tying with 2012 for the highest-scoring opening week since the 1970 merger. Correlation isn't necessarily causation, but offenses went under center at the highest rate in more than a decade and didn't exactly suffer for their choice. OK, so now you know how we got to what we saw in Week 1. But what benefits are teams hoping to realize from moving under center? How does it fit what defenses are showing? And what are the trade-offs? The 'why' of going under center If you ask NFL coaches why offenses are going under center, one answer invariably comes up: They want a more diverse and unpredictable run game. There are advantages to operating out of the shotgun, and we'll get to them in a minute, but one of the disadvantages comes with what teams are able (or unable) to do on the ground. In the shotgun, running backs line up to the side of the quarterback, which both limits the types of run concepts offenses can run and makes the side to which they'll ultimately run more predictable. Offensive architects have gotten more creative with motion to try to disguise some of those concepts, with blockers motioning in one direction pre-snap before immediately turning around and attempting to kick out a defender post-snap, but there are concepts where the timing just doesn't really work from shotgun. Take last season's Seahawks, for example. Under center, Seattle ran all kinds of concepts, including inside zone and outside zone, power, counter, duo and a handful of other run schemes. When the Seahawks were in the pistol or shotgun, though, their run game (and the play-action attack that resulted) was almost always built around counter. If you can nail down what a team's going to run by where the running back lines up, you can limit some of its offensive creativity. Under center, the RB lines up directly behind the quarterback, which allows offenses to retain the ability to run to either side without needing to realign or shift personnel. It also helps create the timing needed to run outside zone concepts consistently and effectively. When Washington drafted Griffin in 2012 and attempted to mesh a Shanahan-style zone-rushing attack around the zone-read concepts the rookie had run at Baylor, the coaches installed the pistol to keep the back -- usually Alfred Morris -- directly behind Griffin as opposed to lining him up alongside him. Morris and Griffin combined for 2,428 rushing yards during their shared rookie campaign, but once Shanahan started working with more traditional QBs, he moved his offense back under center and stayed there more often than most other coaches. That Shanahan zone running game also features in here. When the Patriots beat the Rams up and kept them from running their zone concepts and their play-action game by lining up in a 6-1 front in Super Bowl LIII , the league started to get away from what had been its most popular and admired run game. The 49ers had already begun to get more multiple with their run game, but the days of plugging in a late-round pick at running back and riding the zone scheme to a great rushing attack were numbered. The Rams eventually shifted their run game from a zone-rushing attack to a gap-heavy scheme, which changed both how they ran their passing game and where they invested in players, notably spending more at guard than they had during the early days of the Sean McVay era. Moving back under center, teams like the Eagles and Commanders have reaffirmed their commitment to that zone run scheme as part of their playcallers' new philosophies. Those teams already ran zone concepts as part of their broader run menu, but during their 2024 lead-up to the Super Bowl, the Eagles ran zone concepts about 47% of the time. In Week 1, with Mannion and new run game coordinator Ryan Mahaffey taking over the attack from departed offensive line coach Jeff Stoutland, the zone run rate rose to 56%. The Commanders jumped from running zone concepts 37% of the time during their impressive 2024 season to 59% in Week 1 this year. Fangio, whose defensive philosophy to slow down those Rams offenses during his time with the Bears informed what the Patriots did in their Super Bowl win, was ready. The now-Eagles defensive coordinator rolled out that 6-1 front for a handful of snaps in Week 1, including a third-and-1 stop of Rachaad White on an under-center rush attempt in the first quarter. While you can run play-action out of the shotgun or pistol, the hide-the-ball hard play-action from under center is also the preference of most coaches. Play-action rates for the two groupings might as well be on a different planet. Just 9.5% of dropbacks out of the pistol or shotgun in Week 1 came with a play-action fake attached. Under center, meanwhile, teams used play-action on more than 75% of their pass dropbacks. While we're seeing more of the straight dropback pass game without play-action than we had in years past, teams are almost always pairing their under-center passes with a play fake. That hard play-action drives better efficiency on passes from under center. Pass dropbacks from under center since 2021 have generated 0.11 EPA per play, while pass snaps from shotgun or pistol have generated 0.04 EPA per play. That's roughly the difference between average plays run by the Bills and Giants in 2025. The vast majority of that difference, though, is a product of simply running play-action more often under center. If we just look at straight pass dropbacks without any play fakes, teams are basically identically efficient throwing out of shotgun, pistol or operating from under center by EPA per snap. Offenses want more play-action to try and manipulate the wide amounts of zone coverage they're seeing from opposing defenses. As recently as 2016, when ESPN's coverage tracking data begins, teams were running more man coverage (55%) than zone (45%). Zone overtook man the following year, and perhaps owing to the influence of those Fangio-style schemes, teams are playing more and more zone each passing season. That zone coverage figure had jumped above 58% in 2025, and in Week 1 of this season, teams played zone on more than 60% of those opposing dropbacks. The quality of that zone coverage has also improved. It's extremely rare to see a team play static, spot-drop zone defense these days. Defenses have prioritized rangy cover linebackers over two-down run thumpers, and every team has gotten better about passing off routes and both identifying and matching to route distributions over the middle of the field. Safeties have improved in masking their responsibilities both pre- and post-snap. Defenses go out of their way to muddy the picture for quarterbacks in a way that simply wasn't the case on a regular basis 10 or 20 years ago. Under-center play-action is a natural response to those zone coverages. It's much easier to move linebackers and create spaces to throw the in-breakers that Shanahan-style offenses crave to hit when you're masking the ball and creating real uncertainty. And play-action is always going to be a bigger threat against zone coverage than man because more defenders have eyes on the quarterback. Man coverage defenders are primarily looking at their receivers, whereas zone coverage defenders are looking at the quarterback. They're far more likely to be influenced by play fakes. play 0:49 Mike Clay: Jaxson Dart outstanding in win over Cowboys What's missing? Naturally, there are disadvantages and trade-offs that come with moving under center. Some quarterbacks liked to be able to see the full field from a distance without being caught up in the chaos at the line of scrimmage. Quarterbacks can work play-action out of the pistol or shotgun while keeping their eyes downfield, which makes it harder for defenses to disguise or change their coverages. With under-center play-action, the quarterback's back is turned as part of the play fake, and modern defenses attempt to use that small window to change the coverage picture for signal-callers. There's one other notable shift that has come with the move under center, though. As my colleagues on "NFL Live" noted this week , going under center is essentially taking the designed quarterback run game out of NFL playbooks. While QBs will still scramble or sneak, so many of the read concepts that players such as Lamar Jackson and Jalen Hurts have run during their time in the pros have to operate out of the shotgun or pistol. Teams are getting more reluctant about using those concepts with their quarterbacks, even if they've been successful in the past. To put that in context, the peak of the designed quarterback run game in the NFL was 2022, when signal-callers around the NFL collectively averaged more than 31 designed runs per week out of the pistol or shotgun. Those plays averaged 6 yards per rush attempt. Nearly 54% of those runs were successes, and they generated 0.2 EPA per attempt. In addition to Jackson, Hurts and Murray, signal-callers such as Marcus Mariota , Josh Allen , Justin Fields , Daniel Jones and Malik Willis were all being used on designed runs multiple times per game. In Week 1 this season, there were a grand total of 11 designed runs from quarterbacks. The vast majority of them were also designed to hit outside (with most teams running some version of what's known as zone read escort, where a quarterback has the ability to hand the ball inside or break outside with a designed lead blocker). While offenses were comfortable running players such as Allen, Cam Newton and Anthony Richardson Sr . on quarterback power, veer, counter bash and other read concepts that hit the interior in years past, virtually all of the limited QB run game we saw in Week 1 was designed to take a quarterback outside, away from the big bodies at the line of scrimmage. The only one who was employing designed runs hitting the interior was Cleveland's Deshaun Watson , who led the league with a grand total of three designed runs during the opening week. As you can imagine, teams are growing more anxious about putting the players with the most expensive contracts on the roster in harm's way. Jackson has missed meaningful chunks of three seasons with injuries, while Hurts potentially missed out on an MVP award and was slowed by the end of past seasons by his own. Allen has somehow been able to stay on the field without missing time, but he was slowed by a broken foot at the end of the 2025 season. play 1:49 Why Stephen A. isn't declaring the Chiefs as team to beat in AFC Even if those injuries didn't necessarily come on designed runs, the extra hits those guys take is going to make any coach or front office executive concerned. Patrick Mahomes sustained a knee injury on a sneak and was knocked out of a playoff game when he was hit while running a speed option. And signal-callers who were drafted with the idea that they could be part of the quarterback run game, such as Trey Lance and Richardson, saw their development irreparably stalled by injuries. (Lance's season-ending ankle injury in 2022 came on a counter read run concept .) Yes, every football player is at risk of getting injured on any given snap, and quarterbacks can suffer serious injuries in the pocket. In years past, teams were willing to trade that increased risk for the benefits of an efficient, effective play. After that 2022 peak, though, the quarterback run game had grown less efficient. Last year, quarterbacks averaged 4.3 yards per carry on designed runs, which was comfortably the lowest figure we have going back to 2016. Their success rate (48.4%) was also at a decade low, while the EPA per play had fallen to 0.1. Those runs are still useful, but they're nowhere near as efficient as they once were. There are a few reasons why those runs are less effective now than they were a few years ago. One is the shift toward zone and toward adding more defensive backs on the field as part of the second level of defense. The speed those players add to the mix and the eyeballs they have on the backfield give teams a better shot at taking down quarterbacks. Edge defenders have also gotten much better at "feathering" read-option plays, where they manage to give credence to both the give or the keep without overcommitting to one or the other. Edge defenders are also being taught to focus on the quarterback at the expense of the running back. There's a better chance of a designed run or a scramble by a quarterback producing an explosive play than there is from a running back, especially if the quarterback is going to be in space or in position to throw as part of a play-action bootleg. We've seen this play out with the outside zone game and its most common play-action pass, which might be referred to as a naked, flood, sail or one of a range of different ideas that all form part of the same family of ideas. In the Shanahan offense, they're most commonly built off the outside zone concept and punishing the edge defender on the backside of the play, away from where the run is going to hit. That edge defender was usually unblocked or only partially blocked chasing down the line, which gave him a chance to catch the runner as they cut back and attempted to get upfield. The boot action fakes the handoff and sends the quarterback in the opposite direction from the run play, where they can scramble or hit one of three receivers flooding the other side of the field. Even when the ball is getting handed off to a running back, the threat of the play-action fake slowed down that backside edge rusher, making life easier for the offense. At some point, defenses faced facts and adjusted. The outside zone runs were still effective, but defenses got better at dealing with them as they faced them on a weekly basis. And while those runs picked up 4 or 5 yards, the play-action fakes that came off the runs were more likely to average 8 or 9 yards per attempt. Defenses instructed their edge rushers to change their plan and ignore the run and go after the quarterback. If he handed it off, they would be down a man in run defense. If he kept the ball, well, the quarterback was going to be running for their life, which would create a sack, cause a throwaway or limit the boot game to a checkdown. Offenses naturally adjusted back and vice versa, and Shanahan tree offenses have various solutions for how to handle that free rusher. But we're seeing defenses make big-picture calculations about what they need to stop and build their philosophies accordingly. Every defense pays lip service to stopping the run, and it's obviously important in key spots, but defenses would also rather allow a 5-yard run than a 15-yard completion. The threat of the play-action pass or of the quarterback scramble -- the two most efficient offensive plays in football -- is going to cause teams to key on the quarterback when there's any sort of uncertainty about who's getting the ball. That has led to more rushing efficiency from halfbacks at the expense of reduced effectiveness from QBs. Is the quarterback run game out of the professional game for good? No. I heard that same idea about a decade ago, after Griffin and Kaepernick had peaked and declined. Newton was still running the ball during his MVP season in 2015, and while he began to break down in the subsequent seasons, Allen, Hurts and Jackson came out of college and made it a meaningful part of their offenses as they emerged as superstars. Thinking about the quarterback read run game (and majoring in operating out of shotgun) as a cycle as opposed to a short-term trend will probably age better than writing it off as a temporary fad. Who made it work? All right, let's run through some prominent teams who either went under center often in Week 1 or suggested they would during the offseason. What did those moves look like? Were they effective? Or was their shift under center more talk than substance? Kansas City Chiefs Under center: 43.3% of offensive snaps I'll start with the last team we saw win during the opening weekend of the season. The Chiefs dominated the Broncos in a 31-10 victory , but just about everything we saw from them on offense was at odds with what things looked like in years past. With a returning Mahomes struggling early, the Chiefs leaned heavily on new running back Kenneth Walker III , who racked up 173 rushing yards in his Kansas City debut. Mahomes, who was expected to be relatively immobile in his first start after tearing his left ACL , scrambled for a touchdown early and was even used on a speed option. Where the offense operated from was also something new for Mahomes & Co. The Chiefs were under center on more than 43% of Mahomes' dropbacks against the Broncos, a single-game high for the team in a Mahomes start. The Chiefs had averaged 21% under center in Mahomes' starts since the beginning of the 2018 season, so they were under center more than twice as often as typical in years past. That decision might be informed, at least in part, by how Walker prefers to operate. As I mentioned during the offseason, Walker averaged 4.5 yards per carry and had a 40% success rate on runs from under center with the Seahawks, figures that fell to 4.1 and 37%, respectively, when Walker got the ball out of the pistol or shotgun. The early returns, at least on the ground, are phenomenal. As my colleague Ben Solak noted during the game, Walker finished with more rushing yards from under center than any other Chiefs back has produced in any other game over the past decade. On the other hand, Mahomes wasn't great as a passer under center, going 0-for-4 with an interception on a play where it looked like Xavier Worthy ran a different route than the one Mahomes was expecting. Over his career, Mahomes' 74.3 Total QBR operating from under center is third in the NFL, trailing only Jackson (81.3) and Brock Purdy (75.5). If he adjusts and the Chiefs are willing to live from under center on a more regular basis, a more effective run game with Walker and the subsequent play-action attack could be deadly for the Chiefs. play 0:35 Is Patrick Mahomes a fantasy QB1 in Week 2? Philadelphia Eagles Under center: 34% of offensive snaps The Eagles didn't morph into an offense from the 1980s overnight, but this 34% under-center rate was the seventh highest of any Hurts start. And the quarterback run game that faded out of the offense during the 2025 season completely evaporated. Hurts had seven carries in this game against Washington -- five scrambles and two kneel-downs. There wasn't even a tush push, as the Eagles ran Saquon Barkley , threw the ball or punted on various third- or fourth-and-2 opportunities. Barkley produced 42 yards on a third-and-2 attempt, running away from Leo Chenal , through the second level and into the open field on outside zone. His other 14 carries produced 41 yards and just five successful runs. That's a solid performance, but it's not the sort of 2024 Barkley the Eagles were hoping to unlock by moving toward an outside zone-heavy scheme. The same held in the passing game from under center. Hurts dropped back five times from under center. Those plays produced three incompletions, a sack and a 64-yard completion to Dontayvion Wicks on a pretty deep ball where cornerback Mike Sainristil lost track of the throw and nearly came to a complete stop in coverage. Averaging 12.8 yards per play from under center looks great in the aggregate, but the Eagles weren't consistent in their first game under Mannion. And as the game wore on, the offense felt more like the tired, disappointing one we saw for most of 2025 than the dynamic 2024 attack. The Eagles picked up one first down in the third quarter, and it took great individual efforts to get the offense going, notably from Hurts converting a third-and-18 with his legs. It's Week 1, and we'll see how the offense operates in the games to come. Will we see more big plays, or will the offense struggle to move the ball consistently? Washington Commanders Under center: 26.9% of offensive snaps With newly promoted coordinator Blough, the Commanders were one of the more publicly insistent teams about their philosophy of getting under center. They really weren't there all that often in their debut against the Eagles , though. The threat of Fangio's 6-1 fronts might have given Blough pause, but the Commanders were actually under center at the league's sixth-lowest rate during Week 1. Trailing for most of the second half, their under-center rate also dropped to 21% after halftime. What the Commanders ran wasn't particularly impressive, either. The under-center run game turned 14 carries into 52 yards, good for 3.7 yards per pop. And there wasn't much of a play-action game off those runs. Jayden Daniels dropped back five times under center. Those snaps produced 21 yards, including a 2-yard scramble and a 14-yard completion to Antonio Williams on a play where Daniels was forced to scramble out of the pocket under pressure. The Commanders ran a slip screen and a flea-flicker from under center, but Week 1 wasn't a great advertisement for the new offense. Blough's unit generated 0.01 EPA per play, which ranks 19th among Daniels' 25 regular-season starts. play 1:32 Should fantasy managers be concerned about Jayden Daniels? Baltimore Ravens Under center: 34% of offensive snaps The Ravens were always portrayed as a bit of a softer transition than some of the other teams making this move. They were still going to spend plenty of time in the shotgun, and Jackson's time as a pro-style quarterback at Louisville would make the switch easier than it would be for other passers. The move to more zone runs would also benefit Derrick Henry , who majored as an outside zone runner during his most dominant stretch with the Titans. Unlike the Eagles and Commanders, the Ravens dominated in the opener. Henry was great against the Colts , producing 130 rushing yards on 19 carries when Jackson was operating from under center. And on an excellent day for the two-time MVP, Jackson showed that he would have no trouble operating from under center, going 6-of-8 for 114 yards. One of his two incompletions was a spike to stop the clock. And while Declan Doyle dialed up only one designed run for his star quarterback, it produced a 5-yard touchdown, with Jackson reading edge defender Arden Key and waltzing untouched into the end zone. New York Giants Under center: 51.5% of offensive snaps Giants fans who were trepidatious about the additions of Matt Nagy and Greg Roman as offensive architects have to feel great about what they saw in Week 1. The Giants were the league's second-best offense during the opening week of the season by EPA per play, trailing only the Bears. Their 58% success rate was second behind the Jaguars. The only reason they didn't score more points was time; the Giants used more time per play than anybody else in the league and had only seven possessions in their 28-20 victory over Dallas . Perhaps unsurprisingly given Roman's experience as a run-game designer, the Giants leaned heavily into the ground game and bigger personnel groupings in their win. They had a combination of at least two tight ends and/or fullbacks on the field for 67.6% of their snaps in Week 1, the third-highest rate in the NFL. They were in 22 personnel (two running backs, two tight ends, one wide receiver) 23.5% of the time. Unsurprisingly, the team that operated out of 22 personnel most often over the past five years was the Ravens, who used it 14.4% of the time, nearly twice as often as any other franchise. The Giants ran the ball 25 times for a respectable 104 yards from under center in Harbaugh's first game as a head coach. Nagy and Roman were thoughtful about how they used Jaxson Dart on designed runs, which Brian Daboll had relied on heavily as he integrated Dart into the offense last season. Dart had only two designed runs all game, and they were both on zone read escort concepts, where he was running to the outside with a lead blocker. As a passer, Dart didn't have a huge game working from under center, going 5-of-7 for 39 yards with a 2-yard touchdown pass to Isaiah Likely . In all, though, the Giants looked comfortable majoring under center, something they ran only 20% of the time while Dart was on the field a year ago. It's a positive sign for their offensive progress, although the Rams might offer a more imposing defense to Dart this week on "Monday Night Football." play 1:53 Why Rex isn't surprised by Giants' win over Cowboys Las Vegas Raiders Under center: 64.2% of offensive snaps Given that Klint Kubiak is a direct descendant of the Shanahan tree and had his offense under center at the second-highest rate in the league with Sam Darnold in Seattle a year ago, it should be no surprise that the Raiders were one of the most under-center-heavy offenses in Week 1. (10:06) Eric Moody Sep 17, 2026, 06:41 AM ET Close Eric Moody is a writer for fantasy football, men's and women's basketball, and sports betting at ESPN. Eric joined ESPN in 2021 after working as a senior fantasy analyst at Pro Football Network. Prior to that, he spent much of his career as a manager at a Fortune 100 financial services company. Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions "Thursday Night Football" features the Buffalo Bills hosting the Detroit Lions in the first regular-season game at the new Highmark Stadium. The Lions and Bills both won in Week 1, but neither defense looked particularly good. Buffalo gave up 31 points to the Houston Texans and Detroit blew a 21-point lead before escaping with a 31-30 overtime win over the New Orleans Saints . I'd be concerned about Detroit's secondary heading into this matchup. Tyler Shough just threw for 410 yards against the Lions, who are dealing with injuries to safeties Kerby Joseph and Brian Branch . Now they have to face Josh Allen , who can beat you through the air or take off running when the coverage holds up. The Bills' addition of wide receiver DJ Moore gives Allen another playmaker to work with. The Lions have plenty of firepower, too. Jahmyr Gibbs should be heavily involved against a Bills defense that had trouble slowing down the Texans. Jared Goff also has top wideout Amon-Ra St. Brown to lean on. The matchup I'm watching is defensive end Aidan Hutchinson against the Bills' offensive line. Detroit needs to make Allen uncomfortable. If he has time to throw, that Lions secondary could be in trouble again. Betting outlook I'm more interested in the total than the spread here. The Bills opened as a 3-point favorite, but that number has moved to 4.5. The total has also climbed, from 52.5 to 54.5. I would have been much more comfortable backing Buffalo at the opening number, but I'm not interested in laying nearly a touchdown now. The total is a tougher decision. Both teams have the offensive talent to put up points, but oddsmakers have already adjusted for that. At 54.5, you're asking these teams to combine for at least 55 points on a short week. That's a high bar, especially with the Lions coming off an overtime game. I'm also interested in how Detroit approaches this matchup. Coach Dan Campbell could lean on the running game to keep Allen on the sideline, which would eat up clock and make the over harder to cash. I liked the over earlier in the week, but at 54.5, I'm staying away. I'm not going to force a bet, just because this game has shootout potential. Notable player props, bets Note: Odds by DraftKings and subject to change. Jahmyr Gibbs rushing yards OVER 87.5 (-112) Matt Bowen: Take the anticipated run-game volume and the big play traits of Gibbs. In the Week 1 win over the Saints, Gibbs saw 29 carries. Big number there. Plus, Gibbs had seven rushes of 10 or more yards. He's a home-run hitter. Take the over on Thursday night in Buffalo. Gibbs receptions OVER 4.5 (+123) Ben Solak: With a huge points total in this game, we should expect a fast pace and easy offense on both sides of the ball. The Lions' offensive line is dealing with major injury. Starting left guard Christian Mahogany and starting right tackle Blake Miller are confirmed out for this game, joining projected starting center Cade Mays , who is on IR. I think Detroit will struggle to run the ball in this one, and as such, I think they'll get Gibbs his touches through the air. DJ Moore to score a touchdown (+150) Moody: Moore led the Bills in targets in Week 1 and ran a route on more than 80% of Buffalo's pass plays. He has already established himself as a key cog in Allen's passing game. Now he faces a banged-up Lions secondary that allowed Shough to throw for 410 yards and three touchdowns last week. I like Moore's chances of finding the end zone. Dalton Kincaid receiving yards OVER 51.5 (-110) Moody: Kincaid led Buffalo's tight ends in snaps, routes, targets and receiving yards against Houston in Week 1. He finished with a team-high 130 receiving yards and tied for second in targets with Khalil Shakir . Detroit allowed Juwan Johnson and Noah Fant to combine for 87 receiving yards last week, and with this game carrying one of the highest totals of Week 2, I like Kincaid's chances of clearing this number. Keon Coleman 40+ receiving yards (+395) Seth Walder: Coleman had just one reception for one yard in Buffalo's Week 1 contest, but he has upside that has me looking at his alt receiving yards totals. The third-year player ran a route on 53% of Buffalo's dropbacks, so the playing time was at least decent. But more important is the mix of routes he ran: 59% of Coleman's routes were verticals (for context, Moore ran vertical routes 35% of the time in that game), and three seconds into Coleman's routes he was already an average of 12.2 air yards downfield, easily the highest among Buffalo's receivers. Against Detroit's weak secondary, I expect the Bills will take plenty of shots downfield, and Coleman could hit this number by hauling in just one of them.

Arizona Cardinals 2d ESPN staff NFL win rate metrics leaderboard: Ranking the best in pass rushing, run stopping and blocking 2d ESPN Analytics play Lions prepare for hostile environment in Buffalo (0:40) Eric Woodyard Sep 17, 2026, 06:00 AM ET Close Eric Woodyard covers the Detroit Lions for ESPN. He joined ESPN in September 2019 as an NBA reporter dedicated to the Midwest region before switching to his current role in April 2021. The Flint, Mich. native is a graduate of Western Michigan University and has authored/co-authored three books: "Wasted," "Ethan's Talent Search" and "All In: The Kelvin Torbert Story". He is a proud parent of one son, Ethan. Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions DETROIT -- To the child waiting in the friends and family tents, it didn't matter the Detroit Lions had just wrapped up an intense two-hour practice on the sunny afternoon of Aug. 10. The moment 1-year-old Romy Isabelle Goff spotted her father, Jared Goff , on the practice field afterward, she immediately threw herself into his arms. Goff then introduced his daughter to teammates and coaches in between chasing her around. Romy, who was born in early July 2025, was too young to regularly attend training camp with her dad last summer. But this season, she and Goff's wife, Christen, were a consistent presence on the practice fields as the Goff family would often spend quality time together once training concluded. As Goff plays his 11th season, and the Lions' Thursday night game against the Buffalo Bills (8:15 p.m. ET, Prime Video), he and others around him have seen a different mindset from the 31-year-old quarterback. Romy's presence in his life has sharpened his focus and supercharged a sense of urgency that was instilled in him by his father, Jerry, a former MLB catcher. From the start of the Lions' offseason workout dates, teammate Penei Sewell said he could sense a different vibe from Goff, and head coach Dan Campbell said he noticed a heightened sense of urgency. "I think it absolutely transitions to the field," Christen said. "I think having perspective and having [an] understanding that there's more [to] life than football really helps you even focus in more on football and what you're doing there because it takes that pressure off that this is your whole life. Like, there's so much more to life. "So he can really, when he's at work, he can focus -- he can put in his time, he can put in his energy and to know when he's at home that nothing's going to change. He has a wife and a baby that loves him, and it gives him the freedom to play more freely, I think, without the pressure of his full identity being wrapped up as the quarterback of the Detroit Lions." In Week 1, Goff helped the Lions get off to a 1-0 start with a 31-30 victory over the New Orleans Saints . He threw two touchdowns, including the game winner in overtime to Amon-Ra St. Brown, which extended his TD streak to 24 games -- a franchise record and the longest active streak in the league. After the victory, Christen posted Instagram photos of Romy roaming the sidelines of Ford Field before the game. She also posted a candid photo of Romy in the arms of her beaming father with the caption: "Sundays are back!" "Your goal is to win the whole thing, and you want your career to go a certain way, and you have aspirations and all these things, but I think she reminds me that there's more to it," Goff said of Romy. "And every time I finish up, getting able to see her and just [knowing] I get to go home to someone who doesn't care. "It makes things a lot lighter for sure." And Goff said the new perspective fatherhood has brought will translate to the field when it matters most. "[Fatherhood] gives you a little freedom. It does," Goff told ESPN. "And I felt like I was in a really good place prior to having her, but I think it just unlocks a new world that you can't really feel until that happens." View this post on Instagram A post shared by Christen Harper Goff (@christengoff) JERRY GOFF UNDERSTOOD exactly what it took to excel in sports. He spent six years in the major leagues as a catcher between 1990 and 1996, playing for the Montreal Expos, Pittsburgh Pirates and Houston Astros. In the Goff home in Novato, California, Jerry instilled a sense of urgency in his son at a young age. "He'd be playing video games like every other kid. I said, 'Let's go out and hit,' for example. ... He would say, 'I'm playing video games,'" Jerry recalled. "And I would just tell him, 'You go play your video game and I'm going to support you there, but somebody else is getting better while you're doing that.' "And that was always my thought when I was training. If I'm not working, somebody else was working and then next thing you'd know, I'd get a tap on the shoulder, 'Hey dad, let's go hit.' He understood." Those lessons ultimately helped Jared finish his prep career with a 39-4 record over three varsity football seasons at Marin Catholic High School in Kentfield, California. He was the first quarterback in Cal history to start as a true freshman, then the No. 1 pick in the 2016 NFL draft by the Los Angeles Rams . "What I have been able to give him, which most dads can't, is the perspective -- when he was younger in particular -- of playing at the highest level," Jerry told ESPN. "And giving him the tools, and he took it and ran with it to know how to prepare for the highest level, and I mean like in work ethic. "I've always said, 'You can't be like the rest of the kids if you want to be the best player, you can't. You can't go to the beach on the weekends every time, you have to be different.' You have to be different if you want to pursue greatness." That pursuit of excellence has become a feature of Jared Goff's professional career. He was traded by the Rams to Detroit in winter 2021 for former Lions star Matthew Stafford just two seasons after leading L.A. to a Super Bowl berth. But Goff resurrected his career in Detroit, leading the Lions to four consecutive winning seasons while becoming one of the NFL's most accurate and efficient quarterbacks. The trade worked out for both teams as Stafford led the Rams to a victory in Super Bowl 56. Now entering Year 6 in Detroit, Goff's focus and standard to win has heightened. "With Jared, things change when the season starts," Jerry said. "It's a little bit of a switch that gets flipped in terms of his focus and attention to detail and just his demeanor. Similar to me when I played [professional baseball]. In the offseason, it's loose and all that, but once the season goes, he's a different cat. He's so locked in. "Yes, the baby is the focal point, love of his life with him and Christen, and I can see there being a sense of urgency a little bit. But there's always a sense of urgency for Jared. He's got one thing in mind, and we all know what that is and that's the ultimate goal." THE LIONS WILL need the best version of Goff if they hope to return to the postseason and potentially bring home a Super Bowl. According to ESPN Analytics, the Lions entered the year with a 40% chance to win the NFC North -- the best odds of any team in the division. And after the Week 1 win over the Saints, Goff reached 39,828 career passing yards, passing Eli Manning (39,755) for the eighth-most passing yards through 11 seasons in NFL history. But 2025 represented a slight step back for Goff. After Ben Johnson left as offensive coordinator to become head coach of the Chicago Bears , Goff posted his worst Total QBR (57.3) since his first season in Detroit (45.5 in 2021), when the Lions finished 3-10-1. Last season, Goff particularly struggled when pressured. He faced a pressure rate of 28.9%, his highest since his first two seasons with the Rams. He also was sacked a career-high 38 times. Doubts outside the Lions building have arisen about his ability to lead Detroit to a title. ESPN analyst and former Lions QB Dan Orlovsky said such questions being asked about Goff are a sign of how far he has come as a quarterback. "I think he's really started to get the national and public appreciation as a player," Orlovsky said. "Like, you hear guys talk about Jared Goff now and it's not just Lions, it's not just [St. Brown] and [ Jameson Williams ]. I think that gives you, whether we like to admit it or not, that just gives you that credibility and that belief. "And when your peers are talking about you, the way I feel like they've started to talk about Jared in the last year or two, I really think it has an impact." And Goff remains hungry for more. The heightened sense of urgency he has felt because of Romy's presence in his life has him drilling down even harder on every aspect of his play, including his leadership. Goff was voted a team captain for the sixth straight season. "I think the biggest thing for Goff is he's taken his game to such a level right now that I feel like he's in this, man, he's up there, I mean, he's up there," Lions coach Dan Campbell said. "And now what I feel is, 'All right, here's my game.' His game's good. It's damn good. It's the mentality, the urgency, the leadership, the, 'Hey man, let's go.' We cannot accept anything less than the best. "He wants to be the best in the league, and he wants to run the best offense in the league. And to get there, we've got to go, we don't have time. That's where I really feel him growing. And every year I felt more of an urgency out of him in that regard, more command, more leadership, and that has to come organically. It can't be forced on somebody, it can't. And so that's great to see out of him." After the season-opening win, Goff came out of the locker room and spent time with Christen and Romy. He kissed both and stared at Romy, then shrugged with a childlike grin, as if he can't believe his luck. Everything that defines success for him was in that moment. "All he cares about right now," said Cam Croteau, Goff's lifelong friend, "is family and close friends and winning a Super Bowl. "That's it."

new_body: Browns vs. Buccaneers (Sep 20, 2026) Pregame - ESPN Skip to main content Skip to navigation Cleveland Browns @ Tampa Bay Buccaneers Cleveland Browns Browns CLE 0-1 , 0-1 Away CBS Tampa Bay Buccaneers Buccaneers TB 0-1 , 0-0 Home By AP Updated: Sep 17, 2026, 12:44 pm Facebook Facebook Messenger Twitter Email TAMPA, Fla. -- — Baker Mayfield has become the leader and face of the franchise the Cleveland Browns hoped for when they drafted him No. 1 overall in 2018. The Buccaneers are glad he’s found a home in Tampa Bay. What did the veteran quarterback learn in his four years in Cleveland? “A lot of things. I think probably the biggest one (is) trying to be the same person each and every day for the guys in the locker room, the people you work with, the staff that you’re around each day, (and understanding) that some things are out of your control,” Mayfield said. “If you’re trying to get it fixed and you’re not worried about the football aspect of your job, you’re probably letting some things slide and fall by the wayside. So, I think controlling who I am each and every day, trying to lead the best way possible and control the offense and, yeah, ultimately win.” There’s more to the Browns-Buccaneers matchup Sunday than Mayfield facing his old team. It’s two 0-1 teams looking to get on the winning track. Expectations are much different for both. It’ll be a surprise if the Browns don’t finish last in a tough AFC North. The Buccaneers play in the weak NFC South where all four teams lost their openers. “I think we got the bad taste out of our mouths,” Bucs receiver Emeka Egbuka said. “We’re ready to capitalize on Sunday. This new opportunity that we’ve been given. First game in the home stadium. Looking forward to seeing the ‘Krewe’ and all the fans out there. Hopefully we’ll put on a show.” The Browns are giving Deshaun Watson a second start with Shedeur Sanders watching from the sideline and waiting for an opportunity that could arrive when the team plays its first home game in Week 3. For now, it’s Watson’s team and the beleaguered QB is running out of chances to prove he can be the Pro Bowl player the Browns gave up a ton of picks to acquire four years ago. “I always expect our players to play well; I wouldn’t put them out there if I didn’t,” Browns coach Todd Monken said. “So, I expect him to play really well. There was moments Sunday that he did, and there were moments we did a really good job offensively, and there were moments we didn’t. There were moments we didn’t coach well enough; there were moments we didn’t play well enough.” Need to know Cleveland (0-1) at Tampa Bay (0-1). When/where to watch: Sunday, 1 p.m. EDT, CBS Latest odds: Buccaneers by 8 1/2 Against the spread: Browns 0-1; Buccaneers 0-1. Last week: Browns lost to the Jaguars 34-10; Buccaneers lost to the Bengals 33-27. Last meeting: Browns beat the Buccaneers 23-17 in overtime on Nov. 27, 2022 in Cleveland. Series record: Browns lead 7-4. Matchup to watch Buccaneers WR Emeka Egbuka vs. Browns secondary. Egbuka had five catches for 63 yards against the Bengals. Mayfield targeted him on the first three plays of the game and just missed on an opportunity for a deep TD pass in that first series. Browns five-time Pro Bowl cornerback Denzel Ward will primarily cover Egbuka when he lines up wide right. Cleveland used man coverage on 38% of snaps in a 34-10 loss to Jacksonville. Egbuka, who has had success against man coverage in his brief career, could go against Tyson Campbell or Myles Harden depending where he lines up. Stats and stuff — Browns QB Deshaun Watson completed 16 of 22 for 205 yards, one TD and rushed for 38 yards in Week 1. He also threw a pick. — Browns rookie WRs Denzel Boston and KC Concepcion combined for 102 yards receiving and a TD for Boston. — LB Carson Schwesinger , the 2025 AP NFL Defensive Rookie of the Year, led team with 10 tackles and had one tackle for loss in Week 1. — Buccaneers QB Baker Mayfield was 23 of 28 for 216 yards with one rushing TD and three fumbles lost. — Buccaneers RB Bucky Irving had 93 scrimmage yards and one TD last week. — Buccaneers rookie LB Josiah Trotter had a pick-6 on Joe Burrow in his NFL debut. — The Bucs are 0-1 for the first time since 2020 when Tom Brady led them to a Super Bowl title. ------ See AP’s full NFL coverage here Terms of Use Privacy Policy Your US State Privacy Rights Children's Online Privacy Policy Interest-Based Ads About Nielsen Measurement Your Privacy Choices Contact Us Disney Ad Sales Site Work for ESPN Corrections GAMBLING PROBLEM? He joined ESPN in July of 2022 after covering the New York Jets for the New York Daily News. He's a former athlete who finished his college career at Louisville. You can catch DJ on ESPN Radio on his show "Talkin' Texans." Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions HOUSTON -- C.J. Stroud declined to address comments former Houston Texans great Andre Johnson made earlier this week questioning the quarterback's body language. Johnson, the Hall of Fame wideout, was asked on the " LGND Talk" podcast by host Kendrick Perkins about what he disliked about Stroud. "With him, and this is just me personally, what I dislike about C.J. is his body language," Johnson said. "His body language is bad." The comment -- given it came from a Texans great -- caught people's attention. Stroud, though, took the high road when asked about it Wednesday. "I respect Dre as a person, I appreciate his critiques," Stroud said. "But I'm focused on this week, going 1-0 this week [against the Bengals ]. I respect Dre, and if that conversation needs to be had, it'll be had." In the past, Stroud has mentioned that he wants to work on his body language. On occasions, when adversity strikes within a game, he has appeared mopey. Johnson, in his podcast comments, said he worries that poor body language by a QB can affect a team. "I think, as a former player, your quarterback having that type of body language is bad," Johnson said. "Because other guys look at you as the quarterback. So, when they see you feeling a certain way, it kind of trickles through the team." Coach DeMeco Ryans, who played with Johnson in Houston from 2005 to 2011, said he wasn't aware of the former wideout's comments. All-Pro defensive end Will Anderson , meanwhile, heard them and vigorously defended Stroud. "I think C.J.'s been doing a phenomenal job since his rookie year to now with great body language," Anderson said. "He's getting guys going, leading that group of guys over there and having enthusiasm and having fun on the sideline. If something doesn't go right, I think he does a good job of bringing everybody back together and centering everybody. We can't really focus on that. Cincinnati's up right now." Stroud had 287 yards passing and two touchdowns in Houston's 36-31 season-opening loss to the Buffalo Bills on Sunday. He also lost two fumbles, one to open the game and one on the final possession, sealing the Bills' victory.

Courtney is a frequent panelist on Around the Horn and host of Best Week Ever and GameNight on ESPN Radio. She also co-hosts The Chicago Bears Podcast on ESPN 1000. She previously worked at the San Jose Mercury News as a multimedia sports journalist. Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions LAKE FOREST, Ill. -- The Minnesota Vikings ' defense is a "one of a kind" scheme that comes with its own set of challenges for Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams . Chicago's home opener Sunday will be Williams' fifth time going against a Brian Flores-run defense. As a rookie, Williams dubbed Flores the "King of the Cover-0 blitz," but that's not always the strategy the Vikings' defensive coordinator deploys. That makes the week of preparation for the Bears' first NFC North opponent especially difficult and "not fun" for the quarterback. "Coach [Ben Johnson] calls this 'mental war' when you go against versus him, and that's what it is," Williams said. "You've got to be able to go out there and bad things are going to happen. You've got to be able to fight back and stay steady. That's one of the biggest things is not allowing his defense and all of that to fluster you and get in your mind. You stay steady and now it's time to go make plays and get completions and when the big ones show up, take them and find them." Flores' blitz-heavy tendencies are difficult to predict. Williams was blitzed on 37.2% of his dropbacks (6-of-13, 36 yards, TD) during Chicago's season-opening loss to the Vikings in 2025. When the division opponents played again in Week 11, Flores sent a blitz 66.7% of the time, which resulted in Williams completing 11 of his 21 passes for 126 yards (6.0 yards per attempt). Trying to predict which strategy Flores will deploy can be a fruitless exercise. "You don't," Johnson said with a laugh. "You try to have answers for everything. He's been in this division three years now, and yeah, I mean you'd like to think he's put everything he could possibly do on tape until you play him next and you realize he hasn't yet. So it'll be something new. There always is with him and that's what makes him such a good coordinator. "It's a great challenge. It really is. You have a lot of fun on game day. Now the week of preparation is not so much fun, but you know, there's a lot of back and forth that goes into it." The Bears enter Week 2 coming off a 59-point performance in a win at Carolina . Chicago scored on nine of its 14 drives, which consisted of eight touchdowns, a field goal, two punts, one fumble and one turnover on downs. When asked about the full potential of the Bears' offense, Williams pointed to Sunday's result falling short of expectations. "Scoring every drive is our mindset," Williams said. "That's the potential of us. That's an internal expectation, that's an internal feeling just of what we have up front, out wide and in the backfield. It's an expectation from ourselves to be able to go out there and score every time and figure out ways to help the defense. That's our part to help this team, help special teams, is scoring points, as many as we can, on as many drives that we have. That's our challenge."

Jenna is a former cheerleader at the University of South Florida and speaks to the consistency of the program as being one of the top best in the nation. Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions TAMPA, Fla. -- Buccaneers senior offensive assistant/pass game specialist Ken Zampese was with quarterback Baker Mayfield just one year in Cleveland, but he saw enough then and now that has him convinced the Browns made a mistake trading him in 2022. "They had the guy," Zampese, who was the Browns quarterbacks coach in 2018, told ESPN ahead of the teams' matchup Sunday in Tampa. "They had the guy and they gave him up." Mayfield faced the Browns in Week 1 in 2022 with the Carolina Panthers , but Jacoby Brissett was Cleveland's starting quarterback as Deshaun Watson was serving an 11-game suspension. The Panthers lost 26-24. This time, it will be Watson on the other side of the ball. "The year we were there, we were one of the best offenses in the NFL the second half of that season, 5-3, in a place that was -- before that season started -- 1-31," Zampese said of Mayfield. "The script got flipped and the city came alive because they finally drafted a quarterback that worked out for them and they mucked it up. They mucked it up." When asked if he thought the Browns shared his sentiment, Zampese said, "Oh, I don't know. It doesn't matter. We got the guy we wanted [in Tampa] and that's what's important." Mayfield went 29-30 as a starter with the Browns, leading them to the playoffs in 2020, where they clinched their first postseason victory in 26 years with a 48-37 win at the Pittsburgh Steelers . He threw for 263 yards and three touchdowns in that performance before losing to the Kansas City Chiefs 22-17 in the AFC divisional round. That was the high point and what Mayfield has chosen to think about from his time in Cleveland. "With any experience, there's ups and downs, good and bad," Mayfield said. "Ultimately, you remember the good more so than the bad -- the first time having a playoff win since '94 there and going on the road and doing it in Pittsburgh. So it's a lot of good memories there. A lot of teammates that are friends for life." But Mayfield struggled with injuries the following year in 2021, including a torn labrum in his non-throwing shoulder sustained in Week 2. He wore a harness to stabilize the joint, but then-offensive coordinator Alex Van Pelt said it affected his throwing mechanics. He also navigated knee and foot injuries. On top of that, Mayfield faced death threats on social media, and public criticism from teammate Odell Beckham Jr .'s father. Mayfield had also received criticism for some of the things he said publicly, such as calling former head coach Hue Jackson "fake." His brother Matthew had also taken to social media to express his own dissatisfaction with the Browns in 2018. "Whenever a quarterback is drafted that high, everything's set up for you to fail. You haven't done this yet. You haven't accomplished this yet. I compared you with this guy in the history of the organization. I mean, goodness gracious," Zampese told ESPN. In March 2022 -- two months after undergoing shoulder surgery -- Mayfield learned through social media that the team was pursuing Watson in a trade with the Houston Texans . He told ESPN's Adam Schefter at the time , "It's in the mutual interest of both sides for us to move on. The relationship is too far gone to mend. It's in the best interests of both sides to move on." The Browns handed Watson a fully guaranteed five-year, $230 million contract. In July 2022, they traded Mayfield to the Panthers for a conditional draft pick. The Panthers released him in December of that year, and he had a brief stint with the Los Angeles Rams , where he "fell in love with football again," playing in Sean McVay's system. That's also where he met his eventual Bucs offensive coordinator Liam Coen -- now the head coach of the Jacksonville Jaguars -- and his current offensive coordinator in Tampa, Zac Robinson. The stint with the Rams led to a one-year "prove it" deal with the Bucs in 2023, culminating in an NFC South title that season and a wild-card playoff victory over the Philadelphia Eagles . He would lead the Bucs to another division title in 2024. An injury-marred season for Mayfield and the Bucs set them back in 2025, but he was rewarded with a three-year, $165 million contract extension. "I think for me it goes back to the faith, looking up and knowing that no matter what happens, if I control what I can control, I'm doing things the right way," Mayfield said. "Obviously I want to win as an ultracompetitor, that's what you want to do at all times. So having trust in that, having faith in that and taking it one day at a time." Mayfield told the "4th & South" podcast this summer that he has had this Week 2 game circled since the schedule was revealed. But in Week 1, he fumbled the ball three times in a season-opening 33-27 loss at the Cincinnati Bengals . When the conversation in postgame quickly shifted to Cleveland, his response was more measured: "Obviously, there's history there -- there's no way to go around that," Mayfield said. Much of his focus this week has been on the details of his performance rather than the opponent. Zampese says he believes that will help him manage his emotions, along with his ability to compartmentalize. "Yeah, it's part of the job. And the guys that don't play the position very long, if you're ruled by your emotions that way, you're going to have a roller-coaster ride," Zampese said. "It's the ability to remove yourself from the ups and downs of that or just use it to provide energy and juice for the next situation to get into rather than thinking of the past and letting it bog you down." Watson was suspended 11 games to begin the 2022 season and fined $5 million for violating the league's personal conduct policy after he was accused by more than two dozen women of sexual assault and sexual misconduct during massage therapy sessions. Two grand juries in Texas declined to pursue criminal charges against him. In 2023, the Browns lost Watson to a season-ending shoulder injury in Week 10. In 2024, in Week 7, he sustained a torn Achilles tendon in his right leg, forcing him to undergo surgery and then a second surgery after rupturing it again in January 2025. He has gone 9-11 in 20 games as the Browns' starter, including a 34-10 loss to the Jaguars last week in which he threw a touchdown and an interception and was sacked five times. It wasn't even certain that Watson would start in Week 2 until new head coach Todd Monken announced it this week. Monken was Mayfield's offensive coordinator in Cleveland in 2019. He says he believes he could have done a better job in guiding the Heisman Trophy-winning quarterback. The Browns finished 6-10 that second season. "I just know the competitor he is, and I've said it all along, I wish I had done a better job in '19," Monken said. "I've said that a lot of times. You've got to own the things you can be better at as a coach. And I'm sure there's certain things that, throughout the course of his life or career, he would look at the same way. Ultimately, I was not here for the rest of it, but I can just tell you that you want your players wired like Baker Mayfield." Monken applauded Mayfield's play -- which he said has been at an "elite level," along with his competitiveness, and the way he has held himself to a high standard and others to a high standard, describing it as "everything you're looking for in a player ... just in a human being in general." Mayfield acknowledged some of his own learning lessons from his time with the Browns, with a particular emphasis on his consistency as a leader. "I think probably the biggest one -- trying to be the same person each and every day for the guys in the locker room, the people you work with, the staff that you're around each day, that some things are out of your control," Mayfield said. "If you're trying to get it fixed and you're not worried about the football aspects of your job, you're probably letting some things slide and fall by the wayside. So I think controlling who I am each and every day, trying to lead the best way possible and control the offense and ultimately win." Zampese praised Mayfield as a leader and called last week's game a "blip on the radar" and said that there's an even more "heightened awareness" heading into this one, with better ball security, not trying to do too much. "He's carrying all of us," Zampese said. "He just got rewarded for the job he's done, and we all have great confidence in him doing an even better job as we move forward. And I know he does too." ESPN's Daniel Oyefusi contributed to this report.

Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions METAIRIE, La. -- New Orleans Saints coach Kellen Moore said he "feels good" about Alvin Kamara 's chance of playing Sunday against the Baltimore Ravens . Kamara sprained his MCL on Aug. 18 in a joint practice with the Dallas Cowboys , an injury that was expected to keep him out for a month. But Kamara returned to practice last week, and Moore said he could have played in the Saints' Week 1 loss to the Detroit Lions . He was a full participant in Wednesday's practice. "I think it was just a matter of time on task, getting a full week's work," Moore said. "I though he did an amazing job to put himself in a position last week to practice really well. And so he's in a great place." The status of defensive end Cameron Jordan for Sunday's game is less certain, according to Moore. Jordan has been out because of a hamstring injury since Aug. 6, and did not return to practice until Friday. He was a limited participant in Wednesday's practice. "We'll see what happens," Moore said of Jordan. The Saints rushed for only 91 yards as a team in a 31-30 loss to the Lions. Newcomer Travis Etienne Jr. carried the ball nine times for 46 yards and also caught seven passes for 32 yards. Kamara also probably would be part of the passing game if he plays. "He's a difference-maker at every position, to be honest," Saints quarterback Tyler Shough said of Kamara. "His physicality, his speed, his one-cut ability, his presence, just in the huddle, just from just all that stuff. He's got the experience and then they have to respect all that stuff. "It'll be good to have him back potentially, and we'll see how we go." Tight end Juwan Johnson did not practice Wednesday because of an illness. Rookie tight end Oscar Delp (hamstring) returned to practice for the first time in several weeks.

Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions FLOWERY BRANCH, Ga. -- Atlanta Falcons quarterback Michael Penix Jr . has not ruled out playing Sunday against the Carolina Panthers . There are just some physical benchmarks he wants to hit first before deciding, he said Wednesday. "I'm close," Penix said. "I know I've been saying that, but it's just a couple technical things that I want to hit, some goals that I have that I want to achieve before I do step foot out on that field." Penix has not played since tearing his left ACL in November. He was just cleared for full practices on Aug. 24, at the start of the final week of training camp. Penix said at the beginning of Week 1 that he was not ready yet for live game action. Cooper Rush ended up starting with Tua Tagovailoa (oblique) also out in a 20-13 loss to the Pittsburgh Steelers last Sunday. On Wednesday, Penix split first-team reps in practice with Rush, who is also dealing with back spasms. Last week, Penix got only scout-team reps with Tagovailoa, while Rush worked with the first team. "I'm working each and every day," Penix said. "And right now I got to be where my feet are. So, today I felt good in practice. I want to keep making strides, keep feeling better each and every day. And that's what it's about. And once my knee feel where I need it to be, I'm going to be ready to play." Penix explained Wednesday that it's taking him a bit longer to come back because this is his third ACL surgery -- he had two on his right knee in college -- and his surgeries were different than most others. When asked why Patrick Mahomes has been able to return already despite tearing his ACL more recently, Penix said it's because it was Mahomes' first ACL surgery. Penix said doctors had to use a quad graft for his surgery, because they already used his patella tendons for grafts in his previous two surgeries. Penix said he also got another procedure done on his left knee for added stability. "So, I got more done to my knee than [Mahomes] got," Penix said. "So, if you look at me after my first ACL surgery in 2018, I was back in six months. But this is my third one. I don't have the same tendons and stuff to use for this ACL graft." Penix made it clear Wednesday that he was not facing mental hurdles, just physical ones. "Mentally, I want to go play, but I'm not going to go out there if I don't feel where I need to be physically," Penix said.
