Cockcroft is senior writer for fantasy baseball and football at ESPN. Tristan is a member of the FSWA Hall of Fame. He is also two-time LABR and four-time Tout Wars champion. Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions Patience you must have, my young padawan.* * Contrary to popular belief, this is not an actual Yoda quote from "The Empire Strikes Back." But surely he said it and was referring to Knockout leagues! Week 1 of the fantasy football season is in the books, and for those of you in Knockout leagues for the first time -- whether the first time on ESPN (it's true for all of us!) or your first time playing the format at all -- you're now experiencing the excitement of seeing that first set of knockout cuts on your league's free agent list. It's a cavalcade of star-caliber players and, in all likelihood, a couple of first-round picks! The temptation to rip open your FAB wallet and spend, spend, spend is irresistible. But ... have patience! Knockout strategy demands playing the long game. Remember, there are potentially 16 more Tuesdays like this from which you can enrichen your roster. Pace yourself. Welcome to our weekly examination of Knockout league cuts and prospective adds. Each week, we'll review the most common cuts across ESPN leagues, and provide recommended FAB bids (by percentage of your team's total seasonal budget) and, where applicable, acquisition strategies for players. Standard league managers: Wait! Don't go! There's a commonality between one-week busts and Knockout cuts. How much should you worry about those dud performances, and are there buy-low opportunities within? The FAB-driven suggestions that follow are designed for Knockout play, but the strategies within can prove every bit as relevant in standard formats. Stick around! Feeling left out? Got knocked out in Week 1? It's not too late! New leagues start every week so sign up and play for free >> A note before we begin: Make Eric Karabell's excellent Monday free agent pickups column part of your mandatory weekly reading. Eric's recommendations also apply to Knockout leagues, especially in the season's early weeks, when the talent pool remains thin and every roster spot is precious. Jalen Coker , whose 33.8 fantasy points were fifth best in the league in Week 1, should be on your Knockout pickups list. In this space, however, we're focused upon the big, just-cut names. Here are this week's 20 most-knocked-out players in ESPN leagues: My favorite pickup of the week Colston Loveland , TE, Chicago Bears (10.5% knocked out, 12th most overall, No. 3 TE): His doughnut was as head-scratching a result as they come, as the Bears scored 59 points and totaled 552 yards of offense, and he paced their receivers by playing 86% of the offensive snaps while running 25 routes. Shrug this one off. If you drafted light at tight end -- a risky Knockout strategy for the early weeks -- consider Loveland's availability a gift. He'll be a key target for Caleb Williams in an offense likely to engage in high-scoring affairs due to the defense's inefficiencies. Recommended FAB bid: 15% of your seasonal budget. (Note: these recommendations assume a team with average needs at every position; a team precariously thin at tight end can and probably should beef up the percentage by 150% -- meaning as much as 22% of the seasonal budget.) If a blue-chipper (ex. Jahmyr Gibbs ) became available in your league, my rule of thumb is to go 25-28% of your seasonal FAB if you're in average need at the position and 30-32% if in dire need. Go get 'em Ja'Marr Chase , WR, Cincinnati Bengals (13.3% knocked out, eighth overall, WR4): Ah, September, a month when temperatures cool, pumpkin spice is in vogue and Chase is nowhere to be seen. The No. 3 overall pick in ESPN drafts has now posted two of his three worst career single-game scores in the past two Week 1s (3.2 fantasy points this season, 4.6 last) and has averaged 5.5 fewer points in September compared to the rest of the season. And while I want to vault him into the "all-in" category, September isn't over yet and the Bengals head to Houston, to face a Texans defense that remains one of the most highly regarded defenses despite struggling against the Buffalo Bills . Oh, and the Bengals have an early bye (Week 6). Chase is a guy to get, but would anyone be shocked if he's right here in this space again next week? Recommended bid: 22%. James Cook III , RB, Buffalo Bills (8.1% knocked out, 28th overall, RB7): The running back to get among potential availables, Cook's Week 1 dud has easy explanations, from the Texans' stout run defense to Josh Allen taking the reins early. That the Bills totaled 36 points and 409 total yards against that defense speaks volumes about the touchdown potential -- critical to his 2026 outlook -- Cook should have. He has a tricky early schedule (DET, LAC, NE, @LAR the next four weeks) and a suboptimal Week 7 bye, but he's also one of the position's best. Recommended bid: 20%. George Pickens , WR, Dallas Cowboys (14.5% knocked out, fourth overall, WR2): The one thing keeping Lamb from challenging for the week's wisest pickup is his "No. 2" status in the Cowboys' offense, if we can even call it that. Pickens matched "No. 1" CeeDee Lamb 's 26 routes run and had three targets to Lamb's five (though two of Lamb's were in the red zone). No. 2 receivers bring a degree of knockout variability concern, but these are effectively 1 and 1A wideouts. I also grade the Cowboys' defense as one of the worst, meaning this is an offense that should pass enough to keep both consistently productive. Recommended bid: 16%. Brock Bowers , TE, Las Vegas Raiders (14.2% knocked out, 5th overall, TE2): Can Knockout managers survive additional absences from one of the game's most highly regarded tight ends? Bowers (knee/meniscus trim) has an outside chance at being ready for Week 2, but he's a long-game add, and a great one at that, especially with the Raiders' distant bye (Week 13). He'd have a higher bid if not for the chance he'll be back in this space next week. Recommended bid: 15%. Drake Maye , QB, New England Patriots (9.8% knocked out, 19th overall, QB4): No, he did not look good in the NFL's first game of the season, but in his defense, it was Week 1 coming off a light preseason for him, and it was a bad matchup at that. Maye is the quarterback to get, even if only barely (over Bo Nix , for me), if you're needy at the position. Recommended bid: 10%. Worthy, with worries Drake London , WR, Atlanta Falcons (15.1% knocked out, third overall, WR1): The Falcons' offense was a mess with Cooper Rush under center. Rush completed only 12 passes, and running back Bijan Robinson accounted for nearly two-thirds of the Falcons' total yardage. London suffered dearly, and it's a concern that QB Tua Tagovailoa (oblique) might still not be ready for Week 2. But let's remember that London averaged 16.6 fantasy points, fifth best among wide receivers, while working with mediocre quarterbacks in 2024 and 2025. He's a long-game add. Recommended bid: 17%. Kyle Pitts Sr ., TE, Falcons (league-leading 15.8% knocked out): Sensing a theme? Pitts is more of a square-peg, round-hole Knockout player because of his historical inconsistency, and his fantasy prospects would be better with Tagovailoa as his quarterback. But, hey, the tight end spot is tough. Recommended bid: 8%. Matthew Stafford , QB, Los Angeles Rams (15.2% knocked out, second overall, QB1): The concerns are obvious, ranging from his age (38), to how shaky he looked in the Australia game, to the travel-related concerns surrounding that game. In Stafford's defense, the matchup wasn't great, and he took a few weeks to find his footing last season, too. Bidding here is long game, though, as he has a tough upcoming schedule (NYG, @DEN, @PHI). Recommended bid: 9%. No thanks Houston Texans D/ST (10.0% knocked out, 18th overall, DST1): We warned you about their early schedule! It doesn't get better in Week 2, as the Texans host the potent Bengals offense, and they also have the Cowboys in Week 4. There's a high likelihood that the Texans D/ST will be high on this list a few times over the season's first four weeks, so save your FAB and invest in streaming options ( Tampa Bay Buccaneers !). Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions BEREA, Ohio -- The Cleveland Browns placed running back Dylan Sampson on injured reserve with a knee injury, the team announced Tuesday. Sampson sustained the injury while returning a kickoff in Cleveland's season-opening loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars . Cleveland also signed Jaleel McLaughlin from the practice squad to the fill the open spot on the 53-man roster. Sampson will miss at least the next four games and will be eligible to return for the Browns' Week 6 home game against the Baltimore Ravens . A 2025 fourth-round pick, Sampson opened the season as the backup to starter Quinshon Judkins and one of the Browns' top kick returners. Second-year player Raheim Sanders , the only other running back on the 53-man roster, filled Sampson's role on offense and special teams after he was sidelined.

Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions What is xTD? xTD stands for expected touchdowns. It is a statistic that weighs every carry/target and converts the data into one number that indicates a player's scoring opportunity. Arizona Cardinals 2d ESPN staff NFL win rate metrics leaderboard: Ranking the best in pass rushing, run stopping and blocking 2d ESPN Analytics Ben Baby Sep 15, 2026, 06:00 AM ET Close Ben Baby covers the Cincinnati Bengals for ESPN. He joined the company in July 2019. Prior to ESPN, he worked for various newspapers in Texas, most recently at The Dallas Morning News where he covered college sports. He provides daily coverage of the Bengals for ESPN.com, while making appearances on SportsCenter, ESPN's NFL shows and ESPN Radio programs. A native of Grapevine, Texas, he graduated from the University of North Texas with a bachelor's degree in journalism. He is an adjunct journalism professor at Southern Methodist University and a member of the Asian American Journalists Association (AAJA). Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions CINCINNATI -- Just before he officially made his NFL debut, Cashius Howell was playing video games with his friends when he thought about something that sounds absurd when said out loud. Before he emerged as one of the best Cincinnati Bengals rookies in recent memory, he was a young defensive end transitioning from playing in the MAC at Bowling Green to being in the SEC with Texas A&M. And in hindsight, that was tougher than getting acclimated in the NFL. "Not like the NFL is easy or anything -- this is the best people in the world -- but I feel like it was more of a struggle trying to get from the MAC to the SEC than it was the SEC to the NFL, if that makes sense." It really shouldn't. But the last few months, including Sunday's win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers , shows why it does. According to NFL Next Gen Stats, Howell matched defensive end Boye Mafe with a team-high four quarterback pressures. While defensive coordinator Al Golden playfully scoffed at the various analytics used to measure players, there was no disputing Howell's immediate impact. "He showed up [on Sunday]," Golden told reporters on Monday. Five months after the Bengals drafted him, it still seems incredulous to some at Paycor Stadium that Cincinnati was able to take the reigning SEC Defensive Player of the Year. Golden recalled that entering the draft, as many as 10 Bengals personnel out of a ballpark of maybe 12 people gave Howell a first-round draft grade. But after the first 32 picks went off the board, Howell was still available. The next day, he went to the Bengals with the 41st overall pick. And since then, the transition has been virtually flawless. Bengals right tackle Amarius Mims , considered one of the team's top ascending talents, said Howell is one of the best rookies he's lined up against in his three years in the league. As good as he looked against the Bengals in offseason workouts and training camp, the real eye-opener came in the joint practice against the Chicago Bears . Howell held his own against Chicago's Darnell Wright , who ranked fourth in the NFL last season in pass block win rate as a tackle (ESPN/Next Gen Stats). That was enough to not only warrant a closer look but validate the same feeling that Golden and others felt during draft weekend. "I don't know he fell to us in the second round," Mims said on Monday. "I don't know how that was possible. But I'm very glad he's on our team. He's going to be a great, great addition for us." Bengals defensive end Shemar Stewart was teammates with Howell at A&M in 2024, one year before Stewart declared for the NFL and the Bengals drafted him in the first round. And he doesn't seem to recall Howell having any learning curve when he arrived in College Station. "I just remember him dogging people out, doing people in," Stewart said with a big laugh. "That's the first thing that comes to mind when it comes to Cash." In his final year at A&M, he was second in the SEC with 11.5 total sacks. And in his first true NFL action, Howell made an early impact. In the first quarter, he shed Tampa Bay tight end Cade Otton before forcing right guard Cody Mauch into a holding penalty. The pressure helped Cincinnati's Kris Jenkins Jr . secure the sack. Howell officially didn't register any stats while playing on 44% of the team's defensive snaps. But his output showed how a defensive lineman can affect the game without ending up in the stat book. While Howell has had a pleasant start, Stewart knows things will get tougher for his fellow Aggie as the season continues. "It's a long year," Stewart said. "It's not like college. It's definitely a lot harder on your body. You're going to be mentally and physically tired because rookies just have a lot more things to do on your plate." Howell is well aware of that. He said playing in the SEC, a conference filled with pro prospects, has allowed him to adjust to the NFL game speed while meticulous offseason work prepared him for the physical rigors of the league. And despite all the praise and early returns, Howell is fixated on keeping a short-term outlook instead of focusing on the potential of a promising rookie season. "I thank God in advance for whatever he has in store for me," Howell said. "Whatever that may be, I'm prepared for it. But I feel like it will be good."

He previously covered the NFL at The Ringer, Bleeding Green Nation and The Draft Network. Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions Who's ready to put their thinking caps on? Big-time offensive scoring was the story in Week 1 of the NFL season, but Week 2 is now right around the corner. What will it bring? Every Tuesday of the NFL season , I'll turn the page from last week to this week with seven things I think. These aren't full-scale predictions -- those come later in the week. They aren't concrete takeaways off the past week of NFL action, either -- those are fired off on Sunday or Monday. Instead, these are the uncertain things. They are things that might be true, but it'll probably take the next few games for us to really find out. And at the bottom, you'll find a few extra half-thoughts ... just those little inklings I'm unable to shake. This week, I'm starting off with my expectations for the schemer heavyweight fight of the century, my theories on the real skeleton key for the Bills' offense and my worry that the first shutout of the season will come this Sunday. Here are seven things I think for Week 2. Jump to: Ben Johnson is Brian Flores' kryptonite Texans' offense will win games Bengals defense is showing promise Kincaid is the Bills' secret sauce Titans will not score in Week 2 Lions have an Achilles' heel on defense Lawrence is league MVP this week Five extra inklings I think ... Ben Johnson is Brian Flores' kryptonite Two heinous crimes were committed Sunday by two of football nerddom's favorite coaches. Let's start with Johnson. The Bears scored 59 points against the Panthers, which is like if you scored 50 points, and then decided to score nine more points. Both running backs D'Andre Swift and Kyle Monangai reached 100 yards and scored two touchdowns, and quarterback Caleb Williams added another two scores on scrambles of his own. And for those tracking Williams' accuracy metrics: 72.4% completion percentage with an off-target rate of only 13.8%. Everything worked for the Bears' offense, which barely left first gear against the Panthers. The Bears will face far stiffer competition in Week 2 against the Vikings and Flores, who rendered an unbelievable performance against the Packers in Week 1. The Vikings blitzed Jordan Love on 73.8% of his dropbacks Sunday -- the highest rate at which any quarterback has been blitzed since the 2023 season. The Packers were in a difficult position entering the game; starting left guard Aaron Banks was hurt, and the camp campaign to build up Anthony Belton at the starting right guard spot was abandoned late in the process. The Packers fielded 2024 fifth-round pick Jacob Monk at right guard and 2024 undrafted free agent Donovan Jennings at left guard. It was Jennings' first career start and Monk's second. In an effort to insulate the young guards, the Packers kept more players in to block than basically any offense over the past few seasons. Love had three or fewer receivers in the route concept on an astonishing 15 dropbacks. Only three quarterbacks have had more such dropbacks over the past five seasons. Flores has little interest in occupying those routes with multiple defenders -- he'd rather throw bodies against the wall of your pass protection and find a weak point. Like water against a dam, it didn't really matter how many players the Packers kept in to protect -- if there was a weak point (which there often was), Flores had a rusher in that spot. His distinctive approach to early-down blitzing breaks the rules. It forces opposing offenses to play a different sport than the one for which they're prepared against other opponents. But Johnson knows Flores well. He called offense against him as the coordinator of the Lions -- twice in 2023, twice in 2024 -- then picked up another two games in 2025 as the head coach of the Bears. Across six matchups, Johnson's team is 5-1 -- the only loss was last season's opener and Williams' first start in Johnson's offense. Over those six games, Johnson's offense doesn't look like a 59-point monster ... but it's clearly better than the average offense against the marauding Vikings coordinator. So what does Johnson do that other teams can't replicate? A few things stick out. The first is communication. Flores' defense requires as much pre-snap coordination between 11 players as any in football -- that's why Harrison Smith is back and so valuable. He can be the coach on the field, changing the playcall after the defense sees the formation. Johnson rises to meet Flores. His offense is as communication-heavy as any in the league, and his group is empowered to make adjustments based on what it sees. Flores wants to get opposing offenses stuck in a bad protection look or run call; Johnson's groups are elite at getting out of such sticky wickets. Williams' pre-snap command, which has reportedly taken big strides through Year 1 and into Year 2 with Johnson, will be tested here. To challenge Flores' reliance on communication, Johnson will randomly snap the football quickly -- no motion, no checking. Immediate snaps. The Bears had 19 quick snaps against the Vikings in Week 11 -- snaps in which less than two seconds elapse between the line getting set and the ball being snapped. It was the most they had in any game last season, according to NFL Next Gen Stats. Second most? The 17 such snaps in Week 1 ... also against Flores. The second thing that sticks out is formational. The Lions loved condensed sets under Johnson, and the Bears have continued that approach. Condensed sets are typically a bad idea against blitz-heavy teams. When you spread out the field, it's easier to identify suspicious defensive alignment that reveals who's blitzing from where. Against Flores and the Vikings, there's no point in trying to riddle things out -- the blitzes are too frequent and too varied. You'll think you're right, you'll actually be wrong, and then you'll be dead in the water. So Johnson turns into the skid. He gets as condensed as possible against Flores. In 2025, no offense had more condensed formations in any game than the Bears in Week 11 against the Vikings, with an average formational width of only 17.7 yards. Teeny tiny formations allow Johnson to throw the ball on out-breakers into a ton of space, to stress the Vikings' cornerbacks who are typically insulated by trap coverages and quick throws. It also allows Johnson to meet Flores' duplicity and disguise with the beautiful simplicity of the running game. With lighter players such as Joshua Metellus and Dallas Turner on the edge against double-teams from extra tight ends and condensed wide receivers, the Bears can grind out physical yardage and set up the play-action pass. pic.twitter.com/x2DPhqCmOP Good Clips (@MeshSitWheel) September 15, 2026 Does Flores have an answer to this approach? Yes ... but not on the chalkboard. The Vikings' first three picks in the 2026 draft were trench picks: defensive tackle Caleb Banks in the first round, on/off-ball linebacker hybrid Jake Golday in the second round and another defensive tackle in the third round in space-gobbler Domonique Orange . Any defense that plays in a division with the Bears needs to be serious about its run defense -- doubly true for Flores, who will never get to third-and-long against Chicago unless he has some run-stuffing hog mollies up front to slow down Swift and Monangai. Johnson won Assistant Coach of the Year in 2024. Second place in voting was Flores. When Flores was a young defensive assistant cutting his teeth in New England, Johnson was doing the same in Miami on offense -- twice a year, they saw each other. These two have circled their matchups like heavyweight fighters for years now, and on Sunday, we get another 90-minute dance in the ring. Bring your popcorn. I think ... the Texans' offense will win some games this year The Texans' defense was a machine last season, and it entered 2026 with all of the Super Bowl hype. Houston just needed an offense that could do enough to win those games in which the defense struggled. Sunday was one such game. The Texans gave up 36 points to the Bills and lost. So did the offense fail to clear its low bar? Technically, yes. But I think the underlying signs were encouraging. In the first game of Nick Caley's second season as the Texans' offensive coordinator, Houston was efficient. Explosiveness has never been an issue for C.J. Stroud -led offenses, but efficiency has been a problem. Against the Bills in a Week 1 loss , the Texans had an offensive success rate of 45.7% -- the ninth-best Stroud start. They had a first-down conversion rate -- how many of their first-and-10s became a new first-and-10 or a touchdown -- of 78.1%, the sixth-best Stroud start. Despite all of the offseason discussion around Stroud, the Texans' spike in Week 1 efficiency was not about the quarterback at all -- it was about the running game. With new running back David Montgomery and offseason additions Keylan Rutledge and Evan Brown along the offensive line, the Texans had a 60% success rate on runs between the tackles against the Bills, their second-best number in Stroud's career. On third/fourth down with 2 or fewer yards to go, the Texans had six runs and five conversions -- they hadn't had more than three in a game since 2023. Over the past three seasons combined, they were 25th in first-down rate and 28th in stuff rate in the same context. They couldn't reliably get to a new set of downs. Now they can. The presence of a functional running game is radically new. Houston ranked 31st in rushing success rate and EPA per rush over the past three seasons combined. It keeps Stroud from feeling as if he needs to make every play a haymaker, which draws out the worst of his play, as we saw last postseason. It also slows down the pass rush. Stroud was pressured on 21.4% of his dropbacks Sunday, per NFL Next Gen Stats. The fourth-year quarterback still committed two brutal mistakes on pressured dropbacks -- a strip sack in his own territory that set up a Bills field goal and the strip sack to end the game. The Texans paid for right guard Ed Ingram largely because of his impact as a run blocker ... but he gave up the first-and-goal quick pressure to Deone Walker that set the Texans behind the sticks. With Braden Smith hurt, Trent Brown manned the right tackle spot -- another superior run blocker to pass protector. He gave up the quick pressure to Greg Rousseau that ended the game. The Texans draw a Bengals team in Week 2 that, like the Bills, wants to play from two-high shells and drop into zone coverage. Buffalo forced two turnovers by Houston; Cincinnati took four from Tampa Bay in Week 1. If Houston continues to struggle with pass protection and ball security on key passing downs, the improvements in the running game won't mean much. But for the bulk of that game, Stroud looked like his old self: calm, poised and aggressive. He drilled a beautiful touchdown to Nico Collins in the middle of the field in a play that was emblematic of much of his outing; Stroud threw 50.0% in-breaking routes against Buffalo, more than any other quarterback in Week 1. If Stroud can be the playmaker with his arm that he has been for much of his career in tandem with a more effective running game, the Texans should have the offense they've long needed to pair with their elite defense -- a balanced approach that gives them ability to hang in shootouts with the league's best offenses. Buffalo was the first test of that. Cincinnati is another great offense with a gettable defense. Bengals QB Joe Burrow has a wicked quick time to throw -- over 70% of his passes were out in under 2.5 seconds against the Buccaneers. That quick game will neutralize the Texans' pass rush some, and Houston's offense will again be called upon to pick up some of the slack. It was nine yards away from answering the call in Week 1, and I find myself full of belief it will answer the call in Week 2 and the games to come. I think ... four takeaways isn't the story of the Bengals' defense Go out and buy yourself a defense. It's just that easy. Pay Bryan Cook and get a forced fumble on Bucky Irving . Pay Dexter Lawrence II , and he'll get the pressure that forces the checkdown to Irving that ends in the fumble. Pay Boye Mafe and get another forced fumble on Baker Mayfield . The Bengals forced and recovered four fumbles Sunday in a win over the Buccaneers. In the previous five seasons, there were only seven games of four-plus fumble recoveries. The Bengals also got high-value takeaways: One recovery was a scoop-and-score, another was in the end zone to prevent a Buccaneers touchdown, and two more were on the Buccaneers' side of the 50-yard line. The Bengals generated 18.6 expected points on fumbles in this game, the 16th-highest in a single game in the past 20 years. It's easy to see a performance like that and scream "regression" from the mountaintops. And there will be regression because fumble luck is just that -- luck. But we can see the forest through the trees and take a look at how the Bengals' defense performed outside of the fumbles. And the outcome is interesting. The Bengals put a blanket on top of the Buccaneers. Mayfield threw 50% of his passes behind the line of scrimmage -- a number that was well higher before garbage time. It's only the 13th game with at least half of the pass attempts behind the line over the past three seasons, and five of the 13 were backup quarterbacks. Cincinnati turned Mayfield -- typically one of our more downfield passers -- into a checkdown machine. How? Team effort. The Bengals consistently found quick penetration from a variety of sources. Veteran defensive tackle Jonathan Allen got a red zone sack on a twist with Lawrence. Rookie second-round pass rusher Cashius Howell drew a flag on a play-action pass protection. Mafe flushed Mayfield into multiple quick scrambles. The Bengals' defensive backfield, as it did last season under defensive coordinator Al Golden, mixed man and zone coverage looks with a ton of middle-of-the-field help. It's hard to get a bead on what coverage the team is in on any given down. Perhaps the Buccaneers wanted to test how well the Bengals would tackle, as Cincinnati was among the league's worst teams for missed tackle rate last season. There were a few odd early checkdowns from Mayfield -- like this second-and-10 in which he has Emeka Egbuka on the option route out of the backfield ... but passes on it to hasten to the RB checkdown. Whatever the agent behind this shallow approach, the Bengals tackled well all game. pic.twitter.com/Mk5V4AbSEv Good Clips (@MeshSitWheel) September 15, 2026 If Cincinnati can be trusted to affect the pocket and tackle in space this season, then the defense is mightily improved. But that isn't enough. The Buccaneers still had a dropback success rate of 52.8% -- better than the Bengals' offense on the day. Mayfield completed 82.1% of his passes and had a 38.9% first down/touchdown rate, ninth among Week 1 passers. Only Lamar Jackson and the Ravens (173 yards) had more YAC than the Bucs (168). When I first watched this film, I was impressed by how well the Bengals covered downfield (and still am). I think DJ Turner II and Dax Hill form one of the better young CB duos in the league. Upon second watch, I wonder if the Buccaneers played too far into the Bengals' hands and should have done more to test downfield windows. The young linebackers can still be moved in coverage, slot corner is a question, and safety Jordan Battle doesn't have great traits defending the pass in space. Houston is next on the docket for Cincinnati, and as much as the Bengals won their game thanks to fumble recoveries, the Texans lost their game thanks in large part to two fumbles lost. The Texans are far from a perfect offense. Their reliance on Collins at receiver should invite shadow coverage from Turner as Golden forces Stroud to beat him with other pass catchers. The theory in Cincinnati -- that the Bengals can force longer dropbacks and consistently pressure opposing quarterbacks -- should work against a Texans offensive line that's only average in pass protection. But without four fumbles, that formula might produce harsher results. The Bengals' defensive overhaul is only in its infancy. The unit should deservedly play with confidence after Week 1 -- especially the new faces. What the defense is in Week 2 won't be what it is by Week 18. I'm excited to see it in a game without historic fumble production. I think ... Dalton Kincaid is the Bills' secret sauce The Bills made waves when they traded a second-round pick for Bears receiver DJ Moore . And Moore made waves in his first game with Josh Allen : five catches, 100 yards and a score -- not to mention a 46-yard pass interference penalty he drew that set the Bills up at the 1-yard line. But Moore wasn't Buffalo's leading receiver in the win over the Texans. It was Kincaid with five receptions for 130 yards. It was the most receiving yards of his career and the most in a game for any Bills tight end since 1967. It's easy to forget how high the Bills' hopes were for Kincaid when they drafted him at No. 25 in 2023. We were in the throes of the flex tight end revolution thanks to a few historically productive years from the Chiefs' Travis Kelce , who finished the 2022 season third among all players in total receptions and eighth in total yards. Mark Andrews was the primary pass catcher for another AFC contender in Baltimore. The Bills wanted some of that. Kincaid was not an immediate success, which glared relative to the rookie sensations of Kyle Pitts Sr . (2021) and Sam LaPorta (2023). We used to say tight ends took time to develop. But if rookies were hitting faster ... why did Kincaid have only 1,100 yards and four touchdowns across his first two seasons as a pro? Whatever the reason, Kincaid's 2024 season was impeded by a PCL injury in Week 10. He played 66.6% of the team's snaps in the weeks before the injury and 43.2% in the games after he returned. That number was even lower (38.8%) in the 2025 season, when Kincaid was limited because that PCL continued to cause him issues. After a full offseason to recover, he entered the 2026 season unabated. One week down, one week healthy. Kincaid played 72% of the offensive snaps in Week 1, his most in a game since Week 9 of 2024 -- the game before his PCL tear. The Bills had at least two tight ends on the field for 50% of their snaps, fourth among league offenses in Week 1. Only these multi-TE sets ... are not multi-TE formations. Kincaid is truly a big receiver by both alignment and usage. He was in a tight end alignment on only three of his 22 routes (13.6%). Only the Panthers' Darren Waller and the Bengals' Mike Gesicki -- both of whom played half as many snaps -- were detached from the tackle more often in Week 1. No tight end took a greater number of snaps out wide than Kincaid's 15. Take a look at this play. Kincaid starts out in a wide alignment, then motions into the formation as the ball is snapped. He gets a free release from the stack and hits the line of scrimmage with momentum. He clears safety Reed Blankenship , who's playing to Kincaid's low hip and is worried about a crossing route. But Kincaid, who can eat up ground and change direction like a wideout, bends this route back to the corner while outdistancing Blankenship -- resulting in an easy pitch and catch downfield. pic.twitter.com/vvM235VTr6 Good Clips (@MeshSitWheel) September 15, 2026 The reason Blankenship is so worried about the crosser is because Kincaid can run them -- and run away from corners when he does so. Here, Kincaid is in a snug alignment in 13 personnel (one RB, three TEs, one WR). Out of the two-minute warning and still trailing, the Bills go for a two-man route combo off play-action -- all their chips in on Moore on a clear out and Kincaid on a crosser. Kincaid beats Kamari Lassiter to the spot, survives contact and makes another defender miss. Thanks in large part to this play, Kincaid ended the day with 42 total yards after the catch and 20 YAC over expectation, by NFL Next Gen Stats' model -- the most YAC over expectation of a single game in his career. pic.twitter.com/svFTve3T0A Good Clips (@MeshSitWheel) September 15, 2026 The only reason the Bills' recent 12 (one RB, two TEs, two WRs) and 13 personnel obsession works is because Kincaid has legitimate receiver skills. It isn't just the ability to run past a defensive back or break a tackle. Kincaid tracks the football down the field better than almost any other tight end. Since the start of last season, he has averaged 9.8 air yards per target, second to Gesicki. He has a 14.4% first-down rate on routes and a 10.3% explosive reception rate on routes. Those rate stats benefit some from Kincaid's limited snap count in 2025, but the point still stands. He does the thing that players at the tight end position aren't supposed to be able to do: create big plays. Watch this catch over Derek Stingley Jr ., an All-Pro corner. Watch Kincaid jockey for positioning as the ball enters its arc, figure out where it's landing with plenty of time to reposition, then elevate and win the ball in the air. This is Tee Higgins -esque behavior. Tight ends don't do this. pic.twitter.com/7U7frMU3fB Good Clips (@MeshSitWheel) September 15, 2026 In that Moore is the shiny new receiver in Buffalo, it is easy to attribute any and all offensive improvement from the Bills this season to his appearance. But I would argue it is the skill set of Kincaid -- who can (1) keep the Bills in multi-TE sets and (2) make WR-esque plays down the field -- that clarifies Moore's role. The Bills were in 13 personnel on 20 snaps against the Texans on Sunday. On eight of those snaps, Moore was the lone receiver. Running 13 personnel forces opponents into base defense and single-high coverages. It makes them predictable and easier to pass against, and Moore feasts at that table -- but only because Kincaid laid it out for him. This particular stressor is interesting as we enter Week 2, in which the Bills play the Lions on "Thursday Night Football." Over the past few seasons, no defense in the league has more willingly played base defense than Detroit (though the Lions were in base only 26% of the time in Week 1, a new wrinkle from defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard). The Bills will still invite that base defense by lining up in multi-TE sets. And this time, when Kincaid is the widest receiver in the formation, he won't have to contend with Stingley or Lassiter ... he'll get Rock Ya-Sin and D.J. Reed instead. The Lions' defense just gave up 410 passing yards to Tyler Shough and the Saints. What do you think it will do against Josh Allen? Four years after the Bills picked Kincaid, we might finally get a view of what they envisioned for him. And if he continues producing explosive receptions at a 70% snap rate, he -- along with Moore -- will reintroduce the verticality the offense has lacked these past few years. If there's another level to find in the Joe Brady-Josh Allen pairing in Buffalo, it's through Kincaid. I think ... the Titans score 0 points in Week 2 I cannot remember a team that looked less functional on offense in Week 1 than the Titans in Sunday's loss to the Jets. I went back and looked at the past few seasons of Week 1 travesties -- Russell Wilson 's Giants had six points in 2025; Daniel Jones ' Giants had six points in 2024; Jones' Giants also had zero points in 2023; oh my goodness, are all of these just Giants games? -- and I still don't remember seeing something I found this particularly problematic. The Titans looked as if they had never played together before. Second-year quarterback Cam Ward was consistently out of sync with his receivers, and his trademark laissez-faire approach in the pocket spelled disaster as he tried to hit open receivers in time. Arizona Cardinals 2d ESPN staff NFL win rate metrics leaderboard: Ranking the best in pass rushing, run stopping and blocking 2d ESPN Analytics Nate Taylor Sep 15, 2026, 02:00 AM ET Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions KANSAS CITY, Mo. -- During player introductions Monday night, Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes entered the field jumping and screaming as fans inside Arrowhead cheered his return from a nine-month injury rehab. Meanwhile, running back Kenneth Walker III , making his Kansas City debut, just jogged onto the field without any celebration. Together, Mahomes and Walker were effective with their legs to power the Chiefs to a season-opening 31-10 win over the Denver Broncos . In their first game together, Mahomes, a two-time league MVP, and Walker, the reigning Super Bowl MVP, produced plenty of highlights, making sure Kansas City never trailed. Mahomes gave the ball to Walker, the Chiefs' biggest offseason acquisition, early and often to reach the red zone on the offense's opening drive. Mahomes' toughness and athleticism were on display on his 10th snap, as he scrambled out of the pocket and dove -- while being hit by two defenders -- for a 15-yard touchdown. His top speed during that scramble reached 15.8 mph, which was 2.5 mph faster than his average speed on rushing attempts last season, according to Next Gen Stats. "Going for the end zone, it kind of gave me that confidence that I can go out there and be myself," said Mahomes, who underwent surgery in December to repair a torn ACL and LCL in his left knee. "I just wanted to play. I had done so much rehab and so much work to put myself in this position. I just wanted to get out there and play. This is what you do it for. "That was definitely the moment, physically, to say all this work has paid off. I didn't feel anything." Much of the offensive burden was taken off Mahomes because Walker's speed and ball-carrying abilities carried the unit. Walker ran through, around and past the Broncos for a career-high 173 rushing yards, the most by a Chiefs player since 2018, when Mahomes became the team's starter. Walker also became just the third player since 2000 to have at least 100 rushing yards in his Chiefs debut, joining running back Kareem Hunt (148 yards in 2017) and Clyde Edwards-Helaire (138 yards in 2020), according to ESPN Research. "It means a lot," Walker said of his strong debut with the Chiefs. "I see the O-line, the way they work in the weight room and the classroom. We showed it in practice, from OTAs to training camp. We just had to come out here and execute and show it." Besides Mahomes' return from injury, another reason the Chiefs had more designed runs (31) than passing attempts (27) was that Kahlil Benson , an undrafted rookie right tackle from Indiana , made his NFL debut at left tackle in place of Josh Simmons , who missed the game because of a lower back injury. Benson became the first undrafted rookie on offense to start in Week 1 for coach Andy Reid, whose Kansas City tenure began in 2013. Through 26 touches, Walker finished with 191 all-purpose yards and two touchdowns. "You never know, going in, how many times you're going to give him the ball," Reid said of Walker. "For him to play the way he did, I thought it was spectacular. It was something you hope for, and you got to see it, where he was the main guy." Walker converted four short-yardage situations, too, including his best highlight, a 60-yard touchdown run on fourth-and-inches early in the third quarter. "He's phenomenal, man," Benson said of Walker, who last season helped the Seattle Seahawks win the Super Bowl. "I can't say enough about that guy. He's a hell of a runner, and we had a lot of fun." Much of Walker's production was generated after contact. He created 101 rushing yards over expected against the Broncos, the most by a Chiefs running back since at least 2018, according to Next Gen Stats. Walker also forced 14 missed tackles, the most by any Chiefs player in a game during that span. After halftime, Mahomes performed better, as he found his passing rhythm. He completed 7 of 9 attempts for 122 yards in the second half. "I didn't play my best, but we were still able to go out there and beat a really good team pretty well," Mahomes said. "The guys around me stepped up." At the top of Mahomes' list of teammates was Walker. "It's just a special ability to run the ball tough between the tackles and then, when he does bounce it, he has the speed to go all the way," Mahomes said. "Once he gets the edge, he's gone."

Los Angeles Rams 2d Sarah Barshop Bad game or bad sign: Which players should you be concerned about entering Week 2? 10h Matt Bowen Facts vs. Feelings: What eight notable Week 1 performances mean for Week 2 1d Liz Loza NFL playoff picture: Updated projections, chances to make the postseason 2d ESPN staff Projecting the 2027 NFL draft order: Which teams could have an early pick? Arizona Cardinals 2d ESPN staff NFL win rate metrics leaderboard: Ranking the best in pass rushing, run stopping and blocking 2d ESPN Analytics play Schrager baffled by 'sluggish' Rams' travel plan ahead of 49ers loss (0:43) Sarah Barshop Sep 15, 2026, 06:00 AM ET Close Sarah Barshop covers the Los Angeles Rams for ESPN. She joined ESPN in 2016 to cover the Green Bay Packers for ESPN Milwaukee. She then moved to Houston to cover the Texans. She came to ESPN after working as a writer and editor for Sports Illustrated. Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions As the NFL prepared for its first regular-season game in Australia to open the 2026 season, careful thought was put into how to get the Los Angeles Rams and San Francisco 49ers the nearly 8,000 miles from California to Melbourne. The league -- with help from the teams -- settled on a Qantas Airbus A380. The planes had 84 lie-flat seats, ensuring each player had a bed on the flight. Each charter flight flew with four pilots, 22 cabin crew and one traveling charter manager on board. In comparison, when the Pittsburgh Steelers flew to Dublin in September 2025, they flew on Aer Lingus as part of a partnership with the airline. A player, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said Aer Lingus was "like Spirit," a low-cost carrier that shut down earlier this year. The player also said that only a handful of players had business class seats, which were allotted by seniority. There are no guidelines in the current NFL collective bargaining agreement on team travel, and there hasn't been much to show there's a correct way to do it. The last two times the Rams played internationally, they flew into the country the day before. The result didn't go their way this season against the 49ers, but it did last season in a blowout victory over the Jacksonville Jaguars in London. Teams currently have the freedom to travel when they choose for international games. It is a topic that is especially important given the NFL's international expansion as the league will play a record nine international games in 2026. The NFL currently has the ability to play up to 11 games outside of North America, including a yearly contest at Wembley Stadium involving the Jaguars based on the current agreement with the NFLPA. What appears to matter to players is the accommodations teams dedicated to travel on domestic and international trips. In February, ESPN obtained the results of the NFLPA's 2026 report cards , which are anonymous surveys done annually that include grades on categories with everything from the team's facilities to treatment of families to head coach and general manager. In the newest NFLPA surveys, the 49ers received a C-plus in the team travel category and the Rams a B. The Steelers, Philadelphia Eagles and New England Patriots were the only three teams to receive an F. The Miami Dolphins received an A, the highest grade in the category. Among the top four teams in the category -- the Dolphins (A), New Orleans Saints (A-minus), Seattle Seahawks (A-minus) and Denver Broncos (A-minus) -- there were common themes about what makes for a positive team travel experience: having personal space and leg room on a flight (including the ability to recline seats to a laying position), the condition of the plane, the amenities available and advance notice given for the team travel schedule. The report cards are based on a survey of 1,759 players (around 80% of the NFL) across the league, administered from Nov. 3 to Dec. 11, 2025. This is the fourth year the NFLPA has conducted these surveys. ESPN spoke with more than a dozen players, coaches and front office executives about "team travel" and the feedback that serves as the basis for the NFLPA's grades. Linebacker Kaden Elliss , who reunited with the Saints after three seasons with the Atlanta Falcons , said he doesn't necessarily need "luxury all the time where you go" when traveling with the team, but that it's nice to feel taken care of by the organization on the road. "It is nice to know that you give everything you can, you put everything you can into it and it's nice to know and it's very apparent when you have an owner that's willing to do the same," Elliss said. "I think [Saints owner Gayle Benson] just has a really awesome track record of, like, we're going to make sure we want to be the best and we're going to be the best in everything we do, including travel." THE LIE-FLAT SEATS were not the reason Niners wide receiver Mike Evans decided to sign with the 49ers in free agency. But it certainly didn't hurt. In early March, Evans reached out to longtime Niners tight end George Kittle to learn more about how the team is run. Among the many topics that came up was plane seating and how the team travels. "He was a big fan of how we traveled with the lay down [seats] stuff and he's like, "Yep, I never had that,'" Kittle said. "And I was like, 'It's crazy, but welcome to the 49ers.'" Evans got an early taste of what travel with the Niners will look like when he and his teammates opened the season in Melbourne. Though the NFL began its international series in 2007, this trip required the longest flight NFL teams have ever taken for a regular-season game. The two teams handled it differently, with the 49ers landing a week before to practice there. Los Angeles spent almost the same amount of time in the air (29 hours) than on the ground (36 hours) in Melbourne. Although the teams made the final decisions, both head coaches said they talked to players about how they would handle the travel. While in Melbourne, 49ers running back Christian McCaffrey and fullback Kyle Juszczyk spent time at the Saint Haven Club, a spa less than a mile away from their hotel. There, the team arranged for players to have access to everything from hyperbaric chambers to red light to hot and cold plunge to massage to acupuncture -- "literally everything" the team needed to take care of their bodies almost 8,000 miles from home, Juszczyk said. "Honestly, we've had more out here than we usually have [at home]," 49ers defensive end Nick Bosa said. The setup was part of the work the NFL and the 49ers did for months in an attempt to make sure the athletes were as prepared as possible to spend their week of travel on the road. The 49ers are no strangers to a weeklong stay, as it is something they've done in recent years to acclimate to their travel schedules. In 2022, the Niners spent time in Colorado Springs, Colorado, before playing in Mexico City in an effort to adjust to the altitude. They'll do that again before their Mexico City game against the Vikings in Week 11. San Francisco has also done the same at IMG Academy in Florida (2019) and The Greenbrier Resort in West Virginia (2020, '21 and '22). When the Steelers flew to Dublin for their Week 4 game last season, they opted to fly on the overnight Thursday to arrive Friday morning before the Sunday game. In comparison, the Jaguars spent the week before they played the Rams last year at a hotel outside of London. The Steelers went straight to the hotel from the airport with a brief window to settle in before practicing at the field on the property. Steelers coaches, a player said, told the players not to fall asleep on the Friday after they landed, a task the player found challenging. That player had previously played in an international game with another team and spent the week in Europe. On that trip, the player said he had a lie-flat seat on the plane. "I think if they're going to have us travel to the other side of the [world] to produce them some money, then I think they should do us the common courtesy to letting us stay the whole week so we can at least experience the place that we're traveling to," he said. "Y'all want us to make so much money for y'all, but y'all don't care about us enough to say, 'OK, well we're going to take y'all out there, then guess what? We're going to take care of y'all.' "I don't know if it's the league owners or if it's the NFL as a whole, but the NFL's always been like that. It's more about how they're viewed outwardly than how we view them inwardly." THOUGH INTERNATIONAL TRAVEL has been top of mind given the recent trip to Melbourne and the Dallas Cowboys ' Week 3 contest to Rio de Janeiro against the Baltimore Ravens , even domestic travel has its challenges. Saints general manager Mickey Loomis, whose team received an A-minus in team travel on the survey, said the team tries to stay in the best hotels it can, but there are cities where that is more challenging. "For example, playing in Dallas and Miami is going to be different than somewhere like Pittsburgh and Buffalo," a former Patriots player, who last played for the team in 2024, said. "And that becomes hard when you're traveling with 53 players, 20-plus coaches, 20-plus trainers and equipment. Right there, you're almost at 100 people -- and then you have IT staff, video staff, all the other support staff, so the number of people you're housing jumps up crazy fast. You need the ballroom space, the capability to host big things, and that changes the hotel you can stay at, obviously. "I just always knew when we were traveling to certain cities, it wasn't going to be at the nicest of places. I think about NBA teams, even hockey, baseball -- NBA teams are traveling with 15 guys. Hockey is 20-something, plus three coaches. In the NFL, you're just dealing with such a large number of people that it becomes logistically tough." The former Patriots player said the ratings in the team travel category are also probably relative to what players are used to when they're traveling on their own. "Players make a lot of money," the former player said. "When they go stay somewhere, they stay at nice places." The Seahawks don't skimp when it comes to hotels -- we're talking Ritz-Carltons in some cities. "I think the investment we make in where we stay is really important," Seahawks head coach Mike Macdonald said. "We stay in great hotels, so we're really spoiled there." WITH THE SEAHAWKS tucked away in the Pacific Northwest, the nearest NFL venue -- the 49ers' Levi's Stadium -- is roughly 700 air miles away. Road games against their other NFC West foes require flights of at least 2½ hours. Thus, they're often at or near the top of the league in terms of miles traveled domestically each season. The organization takes steps -- and pulls out the checkbook -- to make the travel less onerous. The Seahawks charter a spacious Boeing 747-481 that includes enough lie-flat seats for every player on the 53-man roster. They will typically leave two days early for road games in the Central or Eastern time zone to help players' body clocks adjust before kickoff. "The commitment to being on three-day trips, that's a pretty penny when you add it up on some of those East Coast trips," Macdonald said."But that's an asset for us. "I think the team enjoys our plane, which was a commitment from the powers that be. So it's just continuous investment in how we do things and kind of putting the players first is a shoutout to the people making those decisions and cutting the check ultimately." Including their victory in Super Bowl LX, the Seahawks are 16-2 away from home in Macdonald's two seasons. Since 2018, when Pete Carroll was still the coach, they're 24-5 in road games that kick off at 10 a.m. PT. That's no accident, Seahawks safety Julian Love said. "It's really critical that we can be prepared for a game if we're traveling east on those 10 a.m. games for us," Love said. "I would say [Vice President of Health and Player Performance] Sam Ramsden, Mike Macdonald, several people high up have been really intentional about the plan and execution. We've got a bigger plane so guys can not feel cramped and their legs can be fresh. The hydration, the nutritionists, [Andrea Vanderwoude and Samanntha Clark] do a great job. It's very clear why. "If that doesn't get an A, I don't know what gets an A." The Seahawks have received an A-minus on the player surveys the past two seasons. WHEN THE NFL'S CBA, which was ratified in 2020 and runs through the next five years, is next negotiated, it wouldn't be surprising to see additional language around how the NFL handles international travel -- especially the frequency and length of trips -- to be part of that conversation. Though Elliss said there is a lot that goes into making a decision in free agency, he does think the report card grades play a part when players are deciding which team to join. "I think it just gives you a tell, especially when the same teams are top or bottom year after year after year," Elliss said. "It just gives you a tell of how the organization's run because you want an organization, if you're going to give everything you can, you want them to do everything they can, and there are some organizations that do and some that don't. And I think the report card makes it pretty evident." Loomis said he pays attention to the surveys because of perception, but he also does his own surveys with players on more specific questions. "The best surveys for me is when I get players from other teams and they're with us for a year, I'll go ask them and say, 'All right, what did you see at other places that we don't do or that you think we can do better?' Loomis said. "And invariably, I don't get very many answers for that. [They'll say], 'No, this is the best place I've ever been.' And you'll hear that. "I talked to [Former Bills guard] David Edwards and David said, there's a bunch of former Saints people in Buffalo, coaches and players, etc. And he said, they just talked so well about the environment, place, culture, the locker room, how you guys handle things, he said it was an easy decision [to sign with the Saints]. So that to me is the right survey." ESPN's Brady Henderson, Brooke Pryor, Mike Reiss, Katherine Terrell and Nick Wagoner contributed to this report.

Arizona Cardinals 2d ESPN staff NFL win rate metrics leaderboard: Ranking the best in pass rushing, run stopping and blocking 2d ESPN Analytics play Stephen A.: Josh Allen, Bills made a statement with win over Texans (2:09) NFL Nation Sep 15, 2026, 06:20 AM ET Close NFL Nation is made up of 32 team-specific reporters who cover the NFL year-round across ESPN.com, ESPN television shows, ESPN Radio, ESPN+ and social media platforms. It was established ahead of the 2013 season. Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions The opening week of the 2026 NFL season is now complete after the Chiefs defeated the Broncos 31-10 on "Monday Night Football." We saw a lot of scoring, as 49.4 points per game tied 2012 for the most in Week 1 since the AFL/NFL merger in 1970, per ESPN Research. But that still led to some close finishes, including an overtime win by the Lions over the Saints and the Bills' dramatic five-point victory over the Texans. How do these teams fit in our updated Power Rankings ahead of Week 2? To form the list, our power panel of more than a dozen NFL analysts evaluates how all 32 teams stack up against one another, ranking them from No. 1 to 32. In addition to our 1-32 ranking, NFL Nation reporters named a non-QB newcomer -- defined as a rookie, offseason acquisition or coaching hire -- who shined in Week 1. From Texans running back David Montgomery scoring three touchdowns to third-round defensive tackle Domonique Orange 's big stop for the Vikings, we picked 32 players and coaches who impressed in their debuts. (And again, no quarterbacks allowed.) Jump to a team: ARI | ATL | BAL | BUF | CAR | CHI | CIN CLE | DAL | DEN | DET | GB | HOU | IND JAX | KC | LAC | LAR | LV | MIA | MIN NE | NO | NYG | NYJ | PHI | PIT | SF SEA | TB | TEN | WSH 1. Buffalo Bills (1-0) Week 1 result: Beat the Texans 36-31 Preseason ranking : 3 Non-QB newcomer debut: WR DJ Moore Moore's five catches for 100 yards were somewhat aided when Houston safety Reed Blankenship went for an interception and missed badly, giving Moore an easy path to a 43-yard touchdown. However, Moore also did a lot of things that didn't end up in his standard receiving totals. He drew a 46-yard pass interference penalty and later an illegal contact flag. He also slapped away what appeared to be a very likely interception for Houston safety Calen Bullock . It was everything the Bills could have asked for when they traded for Moore in March. -- Aaron Schatz 2. Seattle Seahawks (1-0) Week 1 result: Beat the Patriots 13-10 Preseason ranking: 2 Non-QB newcomer debut: S Rodney Thomas II Rookie running back Jadarian Price had a solid debut, but Thomas gets the nod for helping Seattle's defense hold New England to 10 points. Starting for an injured Ty Okada , Thomas had a pass breakup that resulted in an interception and an open-field tackle on consecutive drives. The plays got Seattle the ball back for drives that ended with a field goal and the tying touchdown. Thomas, a former starter with the Colts, signed a one-year, $1.4 million deal with the Seahawks and began on the practice squad. -- Brady Henderson 3. Baltimore Ravens (1-0) Week 1 result: Beat the Colts 41-23 Preseason ranking: 8 Non-QB newcomer debut: Offensive coordinator Declan Doyle In his first game as Baltimore's offensive playcaller, Doyle kept the Colts on their heels by putting quarterback Lamar Jackson under center and using play-action. The result? For the first time in the Ravens' 31-year history, they had a 300-yard passer (Jackson), a 150-yard receiver ( Zay Flowers ) and a 100-yard rusher ( Derrick Henry ) in the same game. There will be plenty of opportunities for Doyle's unit to put up more points. Over the next seven games, Baltimore faces five teams -- the Saints, Cowboys, Browns, Bengals and Bills -- who allowed 27-plus points in Week 1. "Man, first NFL game, [he] came out of the gates on fire," Ravens head coach Jesse Minter said of Doyle. -- Jamison Hensley 4. Los Angeles Rams (0-1) Week 1 result: Lost to the 49ers 27-7 Preseason ranking: 1 Non-QB newcomer debut: CB Trent McDuffie The Rams traded four draft picks for the All-Pro cornerback in March as part of their effort to rehaul their CB room. According to NFL Next Gen Stats, McDuffie allowed only two receptions for 22 yards on four targets in Week 1, including two passes defensed. One of the passes defensed came in the first quarter, when McDuffie broke up a pass intended for Niners tight end George Kittle . McDuffie intercepted the ball but was just out of bounds. -- Sarah Barshop 5. San Francisco 49ers (1-0) Week 1 result: Beat the Rams 27-7 Preseason ranking: 9 Non-QB newcomer debut: WR Mike Evans Defensive tackle Osa Odighizuwa was also impactful in his Niners debut, but it's hard to argue with Evans' production. He finished with six receptions for 49 yards and a touchdown, and each of those catches somehow went for either a first down or a score. That gave him the most receiving first downs by any player in a team debut since the Rams' Puka Nacua had six in 2023. Evans signed a three-year deal with the 49ers in free agency. -- Nick Wagoner 6. Philadelphia Eagles (1-0) Week 1 result: Beat the Commanders 24-22 Preseason ranking: 5 Non-QB newcomer debut: WR Dontayvion Wicks Wicks had two catches for 73 yards and a touchdown against the Commanders. His 64-yard catch-and-run in the first half marked the longest reception of his career, providing a much-needed spark to the Eagles' new-look offense. Wicks, acquired via trade from the Packers in April, has assumed the role of WR2 behind DeVonta Smith . QB Jalen Hurts and Wicks built a rapport over the spring and summer, and it translated to Week 1. -- Tim McManus 7. Chicago Bears (1-0) Week 1 result: Beat the Panthers 59-37 Preseason ranking: 12 Non-QB newcomer debut: WR Kalif Raymond The veteran wideout led the Bears with eight catches on nine targets for 84 yards. Five of his receptions came on third down, demonstrating the trust quarterback Caleb Williams quickly built with Raymond after he signed a one-year deal in March. Perhaps the moment most emblematic of his buy-in for what coach Ben Johnson asks of his offensive players is the block Raymond had during running back Kyle Monangai 's 61-yard touchdown in the third quarter. -- Courtney Cronin play 1:03 Bruschi, Rex marvel at Bears after big offensive game in Week 1 8. Kansas City Chiefs (1-0) Week 1 result: Beat the Broncos 31-10 Preseason ranking: 13 Non-QB newcomer debut: RB Kenneth Walker III For one game at least, Walker was everything the Chiefs could've hoped for, bringing more explosive highlights to their rushing attack. Walker produced a career-high 173 rushing yards, with his best moment being a breakaway 60-yard touchdown on fourth-and-inches early in the third quarter. His best trait against the Broncos was his elusiveness, as he forced 14 missed tackles, the most by any Chiefs player in a game since 2018. Walker caught a short touchdown pass, too. -- Nate Taylor 9. Denver Broncos (0-1) Week 1 result: Lost to the Chiefs 31-10 Preseason ranking: 4 Non-QB newcomer debut: RB Jonah Coleman You know it was a bad opener -- and the three-touchdown loss to the Chiefs was brutal -- when Coleman's 27-yard kickoff return made him the best non-quarterback newcomer. It was that kind of night for a team that returned more players from last season than any other in the league. Jaylen Waddle had one catch for 2 yards, safety Tycen Anderson had one tackle and Coleman was the only rookie in uniform for the game. -- Jeff Legwold 10. New England Patriots (0-1) Week 1 result: Lost to the Seahawks 13-10 Preseason ranking: 6 Non-QB newcomer debut: Edge rusher Dre'Mont Jones Signed to a three-year, $36.5 million deal in free agency, the eight-year veteran totaled four QB hits, one sack and two tackles. He was generally a solid presence setting the edge in the running game, as well. The Patriots targeted Jones over retaining K'Lavon Chaisson , who led the team with 7.5 sacks last season. Runner-up choice: sixth-round rookie linebacker Namdi Obiazor (TCU), who led the team with three special teams tackles, including one on the opening kickoff. -- Mike Reiss 11. Houston Texans (0-1) Week 1 result: Lost to the Bills 36-31 Preseason ranking: 10 Non-QB newcomer debut: RB David Montgomery Montgomery, who was acquired via trade from the Lions in March, finished with the most touchdowns in a debut in Texans franchise history. He had three touchdowns and 79 total yards (60 rushing and 19 receiving), as Houston scored its most points in a season opener under coach DeMeco Ryans. Overall, the Texans finished with 124 rushing yards on 32 carries, which helped create more passing lanes for quarterback C.J. Stroud en route to 287 passing yards. Montgomery said, "That's going to be our identity." -- DJ Bien-Aime 12. Detroit Lions (1-0) Week 1 result: Beat the Saints 31-30 (OT) Preseason ranking: 11 Non-QB newcomer debut: OC Drew Petzing Week 1 certainly wasn't pretty, but Petzing's offense looked like a well-oiled machine as it marched downfield for a 10-play, 70-yard drive in overtime that was capped by a 4-yard touchdown grab from WR Amon-Ra St. Brown . Petzing spent his past three seasons in Arizona, and in his Lions debut, he helped RB Jahmyr Gibbs record a career-high 34 touches. Quarterback Jared Goff thought Petzing "adjusted good" and "settled us down when we needed it and got us into the right plays." -- Eric Woodyard 13. Jacksonville Jaguars (1-0) Week 1 result: Beat the Browns 34-10 Preseason ranking: 17 Non-QB newcomer debut: LG Emmanuel Pregnon Pregnon allowed only one QB pressure on 25 pass-block snaps in Week 1. That 4% pressure rate was tied with left tackle Anton Harrison for the best of any Jaguars offensive lineman. Pregnon, a third-round pick out of Oregon, didn't move into the starting lineup until the second half of training camp. He was impressive enough that the Jaguars moved starting left guard Ezra Cleveland to right guard just to get Pregnon on the field. -- Michael DiRocco 14. Green Bay Packers (0-1) Week 1 result: Lost to the Vikings 39-22 Preseason ranking: 7 Non-QB newcomer debut: K Trey Smack How about a 59-yarder for your first NFL field goal? Smack nailed it in the first quarter against the Vikings. He made all of his field goal attempts, also hitting from 43 and 26 yards. He even made a 40-yarder that coach Matt LaFleur took off the board because of a penalty on the Vikings. Smack's only miscues were a missed extra point attempt and one kickoff into the end zone. -- Rob Demovsky 15. Cincinnati Bengals (1-0) Week 1 result: Beat the Buccaneers 33-27 Preseason ranking: 16 Non-QB newcomer debut: Edge Boye Mafe Mafe showed why he was Cincinnati's first big free agent signing with a sack, a forced fumble and a fumble recovery against Tampa Bay. According to NFL Next Gen Stats, he tied rookie edge rusher Cashius Howell with a team-high four pressures. Mafe made the most of his one-on-one matchups and provided solid early returns for Cincinnati's revamped front. He led all Bengals defensive linemen with 37 snaps. On a unit that will be rotated heavily this season, Mafe appears to be leading the charge on the edge. -- Ben Baby 16. Dallas Cowboys (0-1) Week 1 result: Lost to the Giants 28-20 Preseason ranking: 15 Non-QB newcomer debut: S Caleb Downs Considering how poorly the defense played, it's strange to give this to Downs, but the 11th pick in this year's draft had a productive debut. And there wasn't an offensive player who fits in this category. Downs finished with seven tackles, a sack and a forced fumble. He played 61 of 69 snaps, splitting time between safety and the slot. With Malik Hooker suffering a fractured forearm Sunday, though, the Cowboys might have to alter Downs' alignment somewhat, even if he is a valuable slot defender. -- Todd Archer play 1:51 Stephen A. to Michael Irvin: The Cowboys didn't show up vs. Giants 17. Minnesota Vikings (1-0) Week 1 result: Beat the Packers 39-22 Preseason ranking: 22 Non-QB newcomer debut: NT Domonique Orange A third-round pick from Iowa State, Orange made a key play in Sunday's comeback victory. With 13:17 remaining, the Packers decided to take a field goal off the board after a Vikings penalty and go for it on fourth-and-1. Quarterback Jordan Love checked into a sneak play, but Orange -- known by the nickname "Big Citrus" -- fought off center Sean Rhyan and stuffed Love for no gain. "If I was a quarterback," Orange told reporters afterward, "I'd try that, too. But they don't know about Big Citrus yet." -- Kevin Seifert 18. New York Giants (1-0) Week 1 result: Beat the Cowboys 28-20 Preseason ranking: 24 Non-QB newcomer debut: TE Isaiah Likely Likely was quarterback Jaxson Dart 's go-to receiver, catching two third-down passes on the game-ending drive to go along with two touchdowns earlier. Overall, Likely caught all eight targets for 78 yards. The chemistry with Dart throughout training camp carried over to the season, to the point where it's easy to see Likely having a huge campaign despite never reaching 500 receiving yards in any of his four years with the Ravens. The performance was no surprise to coach John Harbaugh. "I mean, we paid him a lot," Harbaugh said with a laugh. "That's what we paid him for, and he did it." -- Jordan Raanan 19. Los Angeles Chargers (0-1) Week 1 result: Lost to the Cardinals 26-14 Preseason ranking: 14 Non-QB newcomer debut: C Jake Slaughter The second-round pick out of Florida was put in a tough position. Slaughter spent most of his college snaps at center, but he competed for the left guard spot throughout most of training camp. When starting center Tyler Biadasz suffered a preseason ACL injury , Slaughter was thrust into the starting role. On Sunday, he had as good a performance as you'd hope a rookie center to have, with no major blunders. He allowed just one quarterback pressure, according to NFL Next Gen Stats. -- Kris Rhim 20. Tampa Bay Buccaneers (0-1) Week 1 result: Lost to the Bengals 33-27 Preseason ranking: 18 Non-QB newcomer debut: LB Josiah Trotter The son of Eagles legend Jeremiah Trotter became the first rookie to record a pick-six and a sack in his NFL debut since sacks became an official stat in 1982, according to Elias Sports Bureau. His pick-six helped turn a four-turnover performance into a one-score game. He also amassed 10 tackles, including two tackles for a loss. -- Jenna Laine 21. Pittsburgh Steelers (1-0) Week 1 result: Beat the Falcons 20-13 Preseason ranking: 21 Non-QB newcomer debut: DC Patrick Graham Even with Falcons do-everything back Bijan Robinson racking up 173 scrimmage yards, it's hard to point to anyone other than Graham. The Steelers' pass rush dominated third-string quarterback Cooper Rush , and the buy-in from the Steelers' veterans was evident. T.J. Watt , who admitted he was stubborn about the idea of moving around in the old scheme, did just that Sunday. Not only did Watt have a pick-six, but he also recorded a sack from each side of the D-line. Graham passed his first test with flying colors. -- Brooke Pryor 22. Indianapolis Colts (0-1) Week 1 result: Lost to the Ravens 41-23 Preseason ranking: 19 Non-QB newcomer debut: RB Seth McGowan McGowan never carried the ball, but he had quite a special teams impact. The sixth-round pick showed promise in training camp as a kick returner and made his debut Sunday. He returned five kicks for 164 total yards. His longest return, a 66-yarder in the fourth quarter, took the ball to the Ravens' 30-yard line. McGowan is expected to get some work behind starting running back Jonathan Taylor as the season progresses, according to coach Shane Steichen. -- Stephen Holder 23. Washington Commanders (0-1) Week 1 result: Lost to the Eagles 24-22 Preseason ranking: 20 Non-QB newcomer debut: LB Sonny Styles Styles finished with one sack, in which he trucked running back Saquon Barkley en route to Jalen Hurts , as well as two tackles for a loss and a QB hit. Styles got caught out of position on a 43-yard touchdown pass to tight end Dallas Goedert -- but that was because Styles and two teammates pointed at Goedert at the snap, expecting a false start call. Styles also took over playcalling duties when Frankie Luvu injured his groin. The No. 7 pick wasn't perfect, but it was a good debut. -- John Keim 24. Arizona Cardinals (1-0) Week 1 result: Beat the Chargers 26-14 Preseason ranking: 30 Non-QB newcomer debut: WR Kendrick Bourne The Cardinals' third WR threat and fourth receiving option had the second-best day Sunday, behind only TE Trey McBride . Bourne signed a two-year deal with Arizona in March and reunited with Mike LaFleur, who coached him in San Francisco from 2017 to 2020. It translated to Bourne catching all eight of his targets for 75 yards. "I'm pretty sure none of y'all had him on y'all fantasy [teams] to play how he played, but just was in the right spot at the right time, a lot of plays," quarterback Jacoby Brissett said. "And we put him there because we trust him there." -- Josh Weinfuss 25. New Orleans Saints (0-1) Week 1 result: Lost to the Lions 31-30 (OT) Preseason ranking: 25 Non-QB newcomer debut: TE Noah Fant Fant, who signed to a two-year deal in spring, made what could have been the go-ahead touchdown in overtime. Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions KANSAS CITY, Mo. -- Denver Broncos quarterback Bo Nix needed just three words to sum up the laundry list of woes in the team's 31-10 season-opening loss to the Kansas City Chiefs on Monday night at Arrowhead Stadium. Nix said it was "pretty pitiful, actually." The Broncos started the evening riding an offseason full of optimism and high hopes, but ended it with one of the worst all-around performances since a 41-10 loss to the Baltimore Ravens in 2024 -- Nix's rookie year. "We just let ourselves down ... we literally gave ourselves no chance to succeed and made it easier for them, point blank, period," Nix said. " ... We don't have a choice but to get better, just a nasty wake-up call." In first-year offensive coordinator Davis Webb's regular-season debut as the team's playcaller, the Broncos found little rhythm, right from an ill-fated opening drive. In their first three plays from scrimmage, Nix was sacked to open the drive and threw his first interception of the season on the third play. The Chiefs turned that into their first touchdown, and though the Broncos answered with their only touchdown drive of the night on their next possession to tie the score at 7-7, the die of frustration had already been cast. The Broncos' offense gained just 176 net yards and didn't have a play longer than 20 yards. And defensively, a staggeringly large pile of missed tackles resulted in Chiefs running back Kenneth Walker III running for a career-high 173 yards in his first regular-season game in Kansas City. Walker averaged 7.5 yards per carry, and his total included a 60-yard touchdown run against a defense that allowed just one back gain more than 70 yards in a game last season. The Chiefs finished with 220 yards rushing, and it was the most rushing yards the Broncos have surrendered in a game since they allowed 234 to the New York Jets in Week 5 of the 2024 season. "We didn't tackle well enough, and then the game became one-dimensional," Broncos coach Sean Payton said. "Really the antithesis of how you beat a good team on the road; it's that simple." And though the Broncos' run defense will be heavily criticized in the days to come, the Broncos' offense will likely bear a bigger brunt. Though Payton has repeatedly said he has significant input in the game-planning and how the Broncos approach each week, Webb's first regular-season game calling plays was not the debut anyone with the team had hoped to see. Payton said his initial impression was there were "a lot of throws, not enough runs." "It starts with me, it starts with our coaching staff," Payton said. " ... Our third-down numbers weren't good. Our rushing numbers weren't good. Pick your spot." The Broncos had just six carries in the first half, and the Chiefs had a two-touchdown lead before running back J.K. Dobbins had carries on consecutive plays. The Broncos also had seven penalties overall; Nix fumbled three times (losing one) to go with his first-quarter interception and was sacked four times -- tied for the most in any game of his career. Nix was quick to point the finger at himself and the other players on offense rather than the plan. "Absolutely, players did not make it easy on [Webb]," Nix said. " ... He was, to me, in the headset; he was a pro with it. ... We called exactly what we prepared for. We just didn't execute, and then we were behind and just literally we didn't a whole lot of good consistently." Nix added: "You learn how important it is not to kill yourself. That goes without saying ... I just felt like penalty after penalty after penalty, nobody has good plays to call when you're in second-and-long and third-and-long. ... We just didn't put anybody in a good spot." Nix pointed to Broncos safety Brandon Jones intercepting Patrick Mahomes ' pass in the third quarter, when the Chiefs had a 21-7 lead, as a point when the Broncos' offense, if it were going well, could have turned the game. Jones returned the interception to the Chiefs' 5-yard line. However, the Broncos lost 8 yards over the next four plays, including a penalty, and settled for a field goal. "We take an interception and literally go backwards," Nix said. The Broncos have a short week to digest it all and prepare for the Jacksonville Jaguars (1-0), who play at Denver on Sunday. "We can act like all that we want. They're still the Chiefs, and they're still a good football team," Nix said. " ... You have to give them a lot of credit, and they wore us out today." "We needed some humble pie for sure," cornerback Pat Surtain II said. " ... Going in all the offseason talk, all the hype about this team, you just got to find a way to cancel all that out and play, you know, just winning football ... got to find a way to bounce back."
