Arizona Cardinals 2d ESPN staff NFL win rate metrics leaderboard: Ranking the best in pass rushing, run stopping and blocking 2d ESPN Analytics play How Caleb Williams showed Week 1 that he's a fantasy 'league winner' (0:56) Bill Barnwell Sep 14, 2026, 07:55 AM ET Close Bill Barnwell is a senior NFL writer for ESPN.com. He analyzes football on and off the field like no one else on the planet, writing about in-season X's and O's, offseason transactions and so much more. He is the host of the Bill Barnwell Show podcast , with episodes released weekly. Barnwell joined ESPN in 2011 as a staff writer at Grantland. Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions There are few joys in sports like the first Sunday of the NFL season . After an entire offseason without professional football, we finally get a flood of Week 1 games all at once. NFL RedZone springs to life for the first time since January. Some years, the anticipation can be more exciting than the actual action, with offenses playing in the regular season together for the first time struggling to find a rhythm. This year, though, offensive struggles were few and far between. Nine different teams scored 30 or more points in the early window on Sunday, just the second time that has ever happened. And with the Vikings unexpectedly making it to 39 points in their comeback win over the Packers , 10 teams scored 30 or more points in all on Sunday. That's the first time that has happened since 2002 and just the third time it has happened on the opening Sunday of the NFL season since the AFL-NFL merger in 1970 (1986 being the other). Some of those big scores were a product of uncommon circumstances. The Lions and Saints went to overtime , when they each scored a touchdown. The Vikings scored four consecutive touchdowns in the second half to come back against Green Bay, with three of those drives starting deep in Packers territory after a big kickoff return and two defensive turnovers, making life easier for a Carson Wentz -led offense to rack up points. A Bengals defense that forced and recovered four fumbles against the Buccaneers took one to the house for a defensive score and set up the offense with two short fields. Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show' Others attempted to keep up in shootouts but fell short. The Texans managed 31 points against a conservative Bills defense in C.J. Stroud 's first start since his playoff meltdown. But after driving into the red zone in the last minute of the game, Stroud was sacked twice on the final three plays, including on a three-man rush that produced a game-ending strip sack. And while the Panthers scored 37 points on a day when Bryce Young threw for 361 yards, well, the Bears scored more points on offense than any team has since the Dolphins went for 70 in September 2023. Today, I'm going to focus on the four other teams that hit 30-plus points and how their offenses got off to blistering-hot starts. The Bears, Bills, Jaguars and Ravens all had high hopes for their offenses heading into Week 1, but they scored a combined 170 points in their season-opening victories. How did they pull that off? Were the defenses more to blame? Or should we be projecting these offenses to lead the league in scoring the rest of the way? I'll run through all four, starting in Chicago, where the Bears heard Ben Johnson say that he wanted to field the highest-scoring offense in NFL history and proceeded to tie the 2019 Ravens in scoring the most points on offense of any team in NFL history in a season-opening performance. Jump to: Bears | Bills | Jaguars | Ravens Bears 59, Panthers 37 While there will still be concerns about the Bears' defense after it allowed Bryce Young & Co. to score 37 points, defense isn't going to matter if you're approaching 60. In their season opener, the Bears' offense scored more points than they have in any other game in the 105-year history of the franchise. They somehow scored 59 points on offense without a single catch from tight end Colston Loveland , the sort of combination that would seem impossible if it hadn't just played out Sunday afternoon in Charlotte. To get there, the Bears produced something that we didn't see from them on offense in 2025: big plays on the ground. For all the things the Bears did well during Ben Johnson's first year at the helm, creating big rushes wasn't one of them. They had just four runs of 25 or more yards last season, tied with the Saints for 25th in the NFL. It took the 2026 Bears all of one game to match their seasonlong total from a year ago. Johnson's offense produced four 25-plus-yard gains on the ground against the Panthers, including touchdown runs of 28 yards (by D'Andre Swift ), 29 yards ( Caleb Williams ) and 61 yards ( Kyle Monangai ). Swift added a 32-yarder early in the game to make it four. The Bears finished with 291 rushing yards on 39 attempts, averaging 7.5 yards per carry. The Panthers don't have a great run defense, given that they ranked 24th in DVOA on the ground in 2025. And defensive issues certainly made life easier for the Bears. Carolina inadvertently doubled Rome Odunze over the middle of the field instead of passing him off from one defender to the next as Williams scrambled just before halftime, leaving a free path for the young quarterback to escape a four-man rush and scamper up the sideline for a 29-yard score. The Panthers also didn't get anybody into the A-gap on Swift's 32-yard run in the first quarter, then missed multiple tackle attempts on the newly extended back before he changed fields to pick up extra yardage. On the whole, though, the Bears were dominant running the ball because they simply overwhelmed the Panthers. Tight end Cole Kmet had one of those games where you can't wait to get back into the building for film review; in addition to making a great catch on a leak concept for a 22-yard touchdown, Kmet made big blocks on Swift and Monangai touchdown runs, driving defenders out of the play to create run lanes. The right side of Chicago's O-line -- highly paid guard Jonah Jackson and budding star Darnell Wright -- had an excellent game. And both Swift and Monangai got more than what was blocked, which wasn't always the case a year ago. The Bears were average on rush yards over expectation per attempt on designed runs last season (NFL Next Gen Stats), but they were comfortably tops in the league in Week 1. Williams made a number of plays with his legs, but he was also just as spectacular as a passer. The 2024 first overall pick has deservedly lived in the dreams of Bears fans all offseason for the memorable moments he had down the stretch and into the postseason in 2025, creating magic in the fourth quarter for the Bears as they led late comebacks. We know Williams still has that capacity to extend plays and deliver passes that few other quarterbacks on the planet can make, and we saw a little bit of that Sunday. The touchdown pass to Kmet was inch-perfect. Williams also extended a play, scrambled, then threw against the grain on a deep out to Kalif Raymond for 28 yards. (Raymond surprisingly led the team in targets, catches and receiving yards.) If there had been any need for late-game heroics, Williams was playing like they would have come. What was really striking, though, was just how in-control Williams looked as a passer, something that wasn't the case on a regular basis last season. The Panthers didn't offer much of a pass rush, as their 16.1% pressure rate was the worst of any team in Week 1, but Williams didn't give them much time to generate one, either. He was really effective early in the game at getting to the end of his drop and getting the ball out quickly. And when Williams did extend plays, they usually produced positive results. With the ball coming out when it was supposed to within the context of the offense and little pressure from Carolina, Williams was also a more accurate passer. His off-target rate was a league-worst 20.2% a year ago, but it improved to 13.8% in Week 1. That was almost exactly league-average. Williams' minus-6.7% completion percentage over expectation (CPOE) was the worst in football among regular starters in 2025, per NFL Next Gen Stats. His plus-11.4% CPOE on Sunday was the third-best mark of Week 1 and the best mark he has posted in a single game under Johnson. Are there elements that probably won't stick? Yes. The Bears went 4-for-4 in the red zone and 10-of-14 on third down, rates even the best offenses in football would struggle to hit for any stretch of time. They started three possessions in Carolina territory, turning those drives into 17 points. Plus, the Panthers helped bail the Bears out, including a roughing the passer penalty on second-and-20 and an offside that wiped off a Williams interception at the goal line. The degree of difficulty will increase dramatically over the next two weeks, with the Bears set to face the Vikings and Eagles at home. While they probably can't count on creating four huge runs every week moving forward, though, there was very little about the Bears' performance that felt fluky or unsustainable. They were an effective team on the ground in 2025, so it's hardly out of the question that they could create more explosive runs this season. Williams looked more comfortable and played more comfortably in his second year under Johnson. If anything, the offense could look even more explosive with Loveland actually figuring into the mix. They probably won't score 59 points every week, but based on what they did against the Panthers, the Bears absolutely look like they can contend to be the best offense in the NFL this season. Ravens 41, Colts 23 The Ravens might have also joined the Bears in topping 50 points if they had more healthy wide receivers to play. Zay Flowers racked up 150 receiving yards in the first half before tweaking his hamstring and sitting out the rest of the game. Rookie Ja'Kobi Lane had a touchdown overturned by a penalty before suffering a wrist injury. By the end of the game, LaJohntay Wester and Chris Moore were running routes for Baltimore alongside Rashod Bateman . By then, of course, the game was already out of reach. If it weren't for a holding penalty on center Jovaughn Gwyn that wiped away that touchdown pass to Lane, the Ravens would have scored touchdowns on each of their first five possessions, gaining 254 yards along the way. And even without two of his top three wide receivers, Lamar Jackson produced a 77-yard touchdown drive and a 43-yard push for a field goal in the fourth quarter, putting any hope of a late Colts comeback to bed. This was one of the offenses I was most intrigued to watch in Week 1. The Ravens are one of several teams moving a mobile quarterback under center more often this season, a concept I'm going to write about in greater detail later this week. The shift wasn't going to be quite as significant for Jackson, who played in a pro-style offense at Louisville, as it was going to be for the likes of Jayden Daniels and Kyler Murray , but this was still Jackson's first game with new coordinator Declan Doyle after a brilliant three-year stretch under Todd Monken. The early returns are impressive. Jackson was 6-of-8 for 114 yards operating from under center Sunday, including a 49-yard play to Flowers out of a boot concept to the left, the sort of explosive pass concept the Ravens were hoping to create off play-action by moving Jackson under center more often. One of his two incompletions was a spike to stop the clock, and Bateman was actually open on a scissors concept on the other, only for Jackson to feel pressure around the right side and get the ball out a tick too late. That timing will come more naturally as Jackson's under center more often. In his first game as his team's primary playcaller, the 30-year-old Doyle delivered on much of the excitement Ravens fans have expressed about the Ben Johnson disciple. He built a great game plan around using Flowers to attack the middle of the field, keeping him away from Indy's top two corners ( Sauce Gardner and Charvarius Ward ) in the process. Flowers picked on slot corner Justin Walley , who was no match. Doyle also got Flowers into the backfield. While that surprisingly included one snap where Flowers lined up at fullback , the more notable play would have been lining him up as a halfback next to Jackson in the second quarter. Flowers came out of the backfield and ran a choice route, which typically requires the receiver to feel the leverage of the coverage and run away into space. The Colts made life easier by simply not covering Flowers at all, and the star wideout took advantage of the missed assignment by taking a short catch 54 yards to the house. Doyle isn't the first coordinator to get his top wideout into the backfield for a choice route -- the Seahawks, for one, put Jaxon Smith-Njigba in the backfield for his touchdown catch against the Rams in the NFC Championship Game last season -- but it's another wrinkle that creates havoc for opposing defenses. Flowers was on pace for a 300-yard game before his injury. If he can stay on the field, Baltimore's top wideout is going to have a massive season. play 0:45 Derrick Henry proved to be 'excellent' fantasy pick with Week 1 performance One of the other advantages of going under center is creating a more diverse, difficult-to-predict run game and more natural angles for outside zone concepts. Those under-center outside zone runs were Derrick Henry 's bread-and-butter in Tennessee, and so it probably shouldn't be any surprise that he excelled in Doyle's debut. Henry ran the ball 24 times for 144 yards and three touchdowns, including a 32-yard touchdown in the second quarter. He had 11- and 22-yard runs on zone concepts during the blowout victory. Jackson's designed run rate dropped last season, and he had only one designed run Sunday. But the two-time MVP showed that he can still make an impact with his legs. Jackson scored from 5 yards out on a pistol zone-read concept, then added scrambles of 16 and 19 yards, the former seeing Jackson duck under two pass rushers before converting a third-and-16 with his legs. If there were concerns that Jackson had lost an athletic step, it didn't seem to be on the tape in Week 1. It was promising to see a new-look Ravens offensive line get off to an excellent run-blocking start in Week 1, but the interior is still an obvious weak spot on this offense. Gwyn, debuting at center and making his first career start in his fourth season as a pro, cost the Ravens a touchdown with a holding call. First-round pick Olaivavega Ioane erased a pair of first downs with holding penalties. A blown assignment between Gwyn and left guard John Simpson allowed Grover Stewart to burst through the A-gap unblocked on fourth down in the red zone, quickly blowing up a play that would end with an incompletion and a turnover on downs. While the Bears are set to face stiffer competition, the Ravens have a soft slate of defenses in the weeks to come. They face the Saints , Cowboys , Titans , Falcons , Browns , Bengals and Bills over the next seven weeks. It's going to be tough to consistently create big plays through the passing game if Flowers is out for any extended period of time, but given that Jackson hit Moore for a 53-yard completion in the second half, there should still be some explosiveness in this offense if Flowers misses a week or two against subpar defensive competition. Bills 36, Texans 31 This game served as a measure of revenge for Josh Allen , who had appeared to be flummoxed whenever he stepped into Reliant Stadium. The Bills collapsed in the second half in a 22-19 overtime loss to the Texans in the 2019 season, with Allen infamously attempting to hit fullback Patrick DiMarco with a go ball on his first pass attempt in OT. The star quarterback went 9-of-30 with two picks in his return to Houston in 2024 , then 16-of-33 for 151 yards with two more interceptions when the Bills lost to the Texans in 2025 . There's no shame in struggling against one of the NFL's best defenses, but over the past two years, Allen had posted a 28.2 Total QBR against the Texans and a league-best 72.8 mark against everyone else. After those three losses in Houston, Allen finally turned things around with his best performance against the Texans on Sunday. It wasn't always pretty, but Allen went 20-of-29 for 334 yards and two touchdowns while adding two more scores as a runner. He also drew a 46-yard pass interference penalty on Kamari Lassiter to set up one of those rushing scores. Lassiter helped get the Bills off the field by tackling Allen short of the sticks on fourth down in the first half, but Allen would have the last laugh. With 1:41 left in the game and the Bills trailing by one point, Allen took the lead back on a third-and-11 by hitting receiver Joshua Palmer for a 34-yard touchdown past Lassiter. It was a perfect throw in an absolutely critical situation, one in which most quarterbacks would be trying to protect the football and keep their team in position for a field goal to take the lead. It made a huge difference, given that the Texans then had to drive for a touchdown instead of simply needing to get in field goal range, where their drive eventually stalled. Of course, Lassiter very nearly won the battle and the game for his team. On the snap before the touchdown pass to Palmer, Allen tossed a lob off his back foot in the direction of DJ Moore , who didn't seem to know that the ball was coming. Lassiter turned to make a game-sealing interception, only for the ball to bounce off his chest for an incompletion. That's an incredibly narrow line to toe as we evaluate Allen's performance and try to draw broader conclusions. If Lassiter catches that, Allen's great game is wasted by a foolish decision late in the contest, and there's still something about playing in that dome that seems to bring the old, dangerous Allen out of the reformed signal-caller. But Lassiter couldn't make the catch, and Allen immediately delivered an incredibly clutch TD pass on the next snap to win the game for the Bills. Likewise, Allen connected with Moore for a 43-yard touchdown on a throw that was nearly tipped away by Reed Blankenship , who might have been a step away from picking it off. In his first game as head coach, Joe Brady did seem to make one change to the Bills' offense, and it turned out to be an important shift. While Dalton Kincaid was efficient on a per-route basis from 2023 to 2025, the Bills simply didn't use him all that often. Kincaid ran routes on 58% of Buffalo's dropbacks when healthy enough to play, averaging 2.0 yards per route run in the process. On Sunday, though, Kincaid ran routes on 71% of Allen's dropbacks, trailing only Moore among Bills pass catchers and marking his highest route participation rate since the first half of the 2024 season. Kincaid caught five passes for a career-high 130 yards, including completions of 35, 38 and 40 yards, beating three different Texans defensive backs in the process. Brady used Kincaid as a split-out receiver before motioning him inside to try to create mismatches and conflict with the Texans' defense. This was his best game as a pro. Kincaid was one of the answers the Bills were hoping to lean on as they dealt with man coverage issues over the past couple of seasons. While teams don't want to play man defense against the Bills out of concerns about Allen's legs, Buffalo's middling receiving corps had left Allen without a receiver who could reliably win against man coverage. From 2024 to 2025, Allen ranked first in the NFL in Total QBR against zone coverage but just 17th against man-to-man defense, a figure that includes his impact as a scrambler. The Texans surprisingly played into that discrepancy on Sunday. Per Next Gen Stats, Matt Burke's defense played zone on 24 of Allen's 32 dropbacks in Week 1. To be fair, Allen torched both coverages, posting a 130.1 passer rating against zone and a 129.7 mark against man, including the game-winning score to Palmer. The Texans had played man nearly 39% of the time in their 2024 and 2025 victories over Buffalo, with Allen going 6-of-22 for 94 yards and an interception against man coverage across those two games. With a healthy defense, this felt like a changeup gone wrong for DeMeco Ryans. Could Moore have discouraged the Texans from playing more man? This was a successful debut for the former Panthers and Bears wideout, who caught five passes for 100 yards in addition to drawing that 46-yard pass interference penalty. Most of Moore's success, though, came against zone looks, with Allen hitting him on a pair of in-breakers against Cover 3 and a flood concept before the 43-yard touchdown against Cover 2. In a game in which the Bills were either ahead or narrowly behind for most of the contest, the Texans also weren't able to pin their star edge rushing duo's ears back and go after Allen. Danielle Hunter knocked away a third-down pass attempt, and Will Anderson Jr . managed a team-high six pressures, but the duo failed to sack Allen once across 32 dropbacks on Sunday. The Texans had two sacks total and managed only three quick pressures after generating seven in both the 2024 and 2025 matchups. Playing one of the league's best defenses in what hasn't been a very friendly stadium in years past, even an average day from Allen would have been a surprisingly effective performance. But with the Bills' defense allowing the Texans to produce one of their best offensive games of the past year, Brady needed something great from Allen. And while Allen very nearly threw the game away, the second chance the Texans gave the former MVP to win the contest was one too many. play 0:46 DJ Moore showed in Week 1 that he has 'immense upside' in fantasy Jaguars 34, Browns 10 I'll finish in Jacksonville, where Trevor Lawrence was facing no such onslaught from the opposing offense. Deshaun Watson ended the first Browns drive with an interception, the second with a dropped interception and the third with a strip sack, while the fourth halted after a fumble by KC Concepcion . While Watson finished 16-of-22 for 205 yards, most of that production came in garbage time. By the time the Browns showed any signs of life on offense in this game, the Jaguars were already up 34-3 and running out the clock. In his 2026 debut, Lawrence picked up from where he left off in the 2025 regular season, with nearly as many touchdown passes (four) as incompletions (five). He was particularly effective and accurate throwing downfield. On passes traveling 10 or more yards in the air, Lawrence went 10-of-12 for 179 yards and three touchdowns, with one of those incompletions coming on a Brenton Strange drop. That 83.3% completion percentage on intermediate and deep throws would have been the second-best single-game mark for a player with 10 attempts or more in 2025, trailing only Jared Goff 's performance against the Rams . While Lawrence played well and coach Liam Coen mixed in some wrinkles to create throwing lanes off play-action, this frankly looked easy for the Jags on offense. From a Cleveland perspective, too many of these throws were pitch and catch, and when the throws weren't perfect, Jacksonville's receivers made great catches, highlighted by a diving touchdown grab by Parker Washington in the first half. Lawrence had just two tight-window completions all day, which I say not as a knock on his performance but as a reflection of how open Jacksonville's receivers consistently got. This felt like a Browns defense that sorely missed departed star pass rusher Myles Garrett and defensive coordinator Jim Schwartz. Jared Verse didn't manage a single hurry in his Browns debut, while new defensive coordinator Mike Rutenberg had a Browns unit that successfully played a lot of aggressive man coverage under Schwartz instead playing a passive, static zone defense. Lawrence faced zone looks on 20 of his 25 dropbacks and wasn't subject to a single quick pressure all game. The Browns blitzed just three times, even while Lawrence shredded their four-man rush. Even without Garrett in the mix, limiting Lawrence to one sack (albeit an 11-yard takedown on a third-and-1) was an impressive performance by an offensive line that loomed as a potential weakness heading into the season. He has covered the Broncos for more than 20 years and also assists with NFL draft coverage, joining ESPN in 2013. He has been a member of the Pro Football Hall of Fame Board of Selectors since 1999, too. Jeff previously covered the Pittsburgh Steelers, Buffalo Bills and Houston Oilers/Tennessee Titans at previous stops prior to ESPN. Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions ENGLEWOOD, Colo. -- When Aqib Talib looks at the current version of the Denver Broncos , he sees a reflection of his football past. "They're us," the former Pro Bowl cornerback said when comparing the current Broncos to the franchise's Super Bowl 50 championship team. "They all love ball, talk to each other, hold each other to it. It's clear as day when you see it." Talib is not the only player from the Broncos' most recent Super Bowl-winning team to see history potentially repeating itself. Dallas Cowboys edge rusher Von Miller -- who was the MVP of the Broncos' Super Bowl win over the Carolina Panthers at the end of the 2015 season -- feels a similar vibe with the 2026 Broncos. "Oh yeah, I see it," Miller said earlier this summer. "They do it the way we did it. ... You can tell they keep it straight with each other." This is turn-back-the-clock stuff for Talib, Miller and those who lived it in 2015. They see similarities between how their championship team was set up and how the current Broncos, who were 14-3 last season and went to the AFC Championship Game , function. The two teams share parallels on and off the field, including institutional support, reliance on an elite-level defense and a penchant for thriving in close games. And these Broncos now hope that the culture created from this formula gets them a Super Bowl win, just like the 2015 team. Denver begins its quest for its fourth title when it plays at the Kansas City Chiefs on "Monday Night Football" ( 8:15 p.m. ET, ESPN/ABC ). "Real winning is in what you might not even see until it's right," Talib said. "It's that attitude, that giving and sharing. You give everything you have, and you don't ever lower that bar on anything, and you hold each other to it every day. And you get guys who can take that accountability. They have it, we had it." When Broncos coach Sean Payton is asked a question about winning, his responses start with words like program, grit and culture. He believes this roster has those things, which is why 45 of the players who were on the 53-man roster for last season's opener still remain with the franchise. That rate of retention is almost unheard of in the NFL and is risky in its own way. But Payton believed this group was good enough to be in the Super Bowl hunt last season because of how it was assembled -- and believes it is good enough again. "Culture is one of those things, we all talk about it, it's like a go-to word sometimes, but to really have it ... it's rare I think," Broncos defensive tackle Zach Allen said. "Some places just say they have it and it's really nowhere to be found. ... If you need to be pushed, or reminded to work, or, like be told to get to work, you're not going to be around here." 'Finding the right people' Payton has often said that the number of NFL teams that can actually win a Super Bowl is fewer than most think because "a lot of them have trouble getting out of their own way." When Payton, who coached the New Orleans Saints from 2006 to 2021, looked to return to coaching in 2023, he searched for franchises that had a "triangle" for success. That involves ownership that provides and understands the resources and infrastructure it takes to win; a personnel department capable of finding the right players; and a coaching staff with the game-day chops and developmental skills to make the most of that talent. And all three of those sides of the triangle must be connected, with a clear vision. "It's still finding the right people, ownership like we have in Greg and Carrie [Penner] and our group, like [general manager] George [Paton] and our relationship," Payton said. "... So when you get that triangle, and you get the ownership triangle ... you have a chance to then do the right things, a chance to acquire the right people." Gary Kubiak, who coached the Super Bowl 50 winner and spent more than two decades with the Broncos as a player, assistant coach and head coach, had a similar mindset to Payton. He described the 2015 dynamic, when he and then-executive vice president of football operations John Elway worked together to form the roster, as a "talent puzzle." They agreed that not all players will fit together, no matter their talent level, if there is not a clear mission about which players are acquired and retained. Talib calls it the process of finding players with "good ego" and avoiding those with "bad ego." "Good ego is you know what you can do ... and we hold up each other to the standard, don't pull down, pull up, no grudges, just real talk," he said. "But you get bad ego, and talent don't mean s---." Many players on both 2015 and 2026 versions of the Broncos say it's that mix that separates them. That the character and accountability have to hold up under stress and the inevitable tests of a season. Kubiak said the current Broncos show the mission he saw in the 2015 team. "It's always about the players,'' Kubiak said. "But the 53 most talented guys just put into the meeting room probably won't win if they don't go together. They have to demand of each other to prepare right, demand of each other to be smart, if that's something you're getting from your group, not coaches, the group, that's special." Payton calls it the "debrief," when the game that has just been played is put through the grinder. He has often said the debrief might be more important than the game itself. No matter the result, Broncos players know what's coming. "Honest talk," Broncos cornerback Jahdae Barron said. "Look at it, assess it, fix it. And that's everybody." Talib, Chris Harris Jr . and T.J. Ward -- members of the 2015 secondary -- said weekly players-only film sessions by the defensive backs were a constant exercise in accountability 11 years back. "All those cliches and s---, it's true; you don't have that 'everyone is accountable' mentality, you ain't going to get the ultimate prize," Kubiak said. "You've got to have it from the top down in the building, at every locker in your locker room." 'Just play badass defense' The 2015 Broncos had one of the best defensive postseason runs in the Super Bowl era. Denver's defense surrendered only one total touchdown pass in three playoff games combined against Ben Roethlisberger, Tom Brady and Cam Newton, that season's MVP. The Broncos had 14 sacks and 32 quarterback hits in the playoffs, and Miller capped off that run as the ninth (and most recent) defensive player to be named Super Bowl MVP. It was the continuation of a regular season in which the Broncos led the league in defensive EPA (by a whopping 17 points), sacks, total defense and pass defense. Denver was also No. 4 in scoring defense. The rugged, make-things-happen group allowed the 2015 team to stay afloat despite injuries and inconsistency from quarterback Peyton Manning. Manning missed seven games with a foot injury and completed a league-low 59.8% of his passes with 17 interceptions (second most in the NFL). "We just felt, and I think as a coach you take it with you into every game, that our defense was going to keep us in it," Kubiak said. "... Even after Peyton was injured and Brock [Osweiler] was playing, we could put things together week-to-week knowing we could play tight games ... and feel good about winning them." The current Broncos have also been led by their defense. Denver's defense led the league in sacks in each of the past two years, setting franchise records in each of those seasons. Edge rusher Nik Bonitto has turned into an All-Pro (14 sacks in 2025), finishing second to Micah Parsons last season in pressure rate among rushers with at least 300 rush attempts. Allen led all players in quarterback hits a year ago, while All-Pro cornerback Pat Surtain II (the 2024 Defensive Player of the Year) leads a deep and schematically flexible secondary. play 1:19 What Patrick Surtain II's pay raise means for the NFL corner market Over the past two seasons combined, the Broncos have allowed the fewest points per game in the NFL (18.3) and have given up the lowest QBR (49.5). They have also led the league in sacks per dropback (9.4%), defensive EPA and red zone defense (opponents scored TDs on only 44.8% of drives). "We want more, we want to get stops, we want to get the ball back for our offense, we want to keep people out of the end zone," Bonitto said. "And we all should feel like we can be better than last year just like we thought we could be better last year than we were the year before." The Broncos finished 12th in takeaways last season, one area where they want to see improvement, but not at the expense of what defensive coordinator Vance Joseph calls "good defense." He has said that tackles need to be made with the intent to knock the ball out and interceptions need to be caught, but those aspects are not as important as third-down defense "or stopping the run or playing tough in the red zone." Better ball luck would help, too. "I know I dropped enough that if I just catch the ones I had, the numbers look different," Broncos All-Pro safety Talanoa Hufanga said. Count Talib as someone who is convinced the Broncos still have the defensive profile to win a Lombardi Trophy. "[Joseph] has been cooking," Talib said. "Cooking like [former Broncos defensive coordinator Wade Phillips] was cooking with us. But VJ's matching up zones, great blitzes. VJ sees the field, he sees the game. "It's what you need, just play badass defense. We did, they do. That gives you that edge, you put a defense with [third-year quarterback] Bo [Nix] , that's everything." 'Be hard to kill' Allen cites performance in a game's biggest moments as one of the prime indicators of a team's culture. Both the 2015 and 2025 Broncos flourished in late-game situations, with the 2015 squad going 9-3 in one-score games and last year's unit setting an NFL record with 11 one-score wins. While close-game success can be fleeting year to year, Payton has often said the "right choices in talent acquisition" can make that performance more consistent, that confidence and belief in these moments come from "demonstrated ability." Several 2015 Broncos players and coaches say their championship run got a nudge in Week 2 that season. In the closing seconds of regulation in Arrowhead Stadium, the Broncos were tied 24-24 with the Chiefs, who seemed content to get to overtime. But Broncos linebacker Brandon Marshall knocked the ball out of Kansas City running back Jamaal Charles' hands, and cornerback Bradley Roby scooped up the fumble and returned it for the winning touchdown with 27 seconds left. "After that, we had a bunch of games, we made plays right at the end," Miller said. "Last seconds, a touchdown on offense, field goal, forced fumble, a sack on defense. We just felt like it would happen and it did." The Broncos had five more wins that season in the final two minutes or in overtime, highlighted by a 48-yard touchdown run by running back C.J. Anderson in an OT win over the Patriots that ultimately decided home-field advantage in the AFC. It's a skill the current Broncos demonstrated last season and believe they have the mindset to repeat, especially as Nix has quickly become one of the NFL's preeminent "tight game" artists. Since the start of the 2024 season, Nix is tied for the league lead with eight fourth-quarter comebacks, with five coming last season. He also led the Broncos to the winning overtime drive in the divisional round against the Buffalo Bills . And every Nix game-winning drive inspires the defense to keep games in range that much more. "It's more about knowing, in those situations, you're going to do the right things to give you the chance,'' Allen said. "Being in the huddle knowing you've done it before and that you have the guys to do it again because everyone looking back at you wants to win more than anything else." Denver will try to play fewer tense games while jump-starting an offense which finished tied for 13th in scoring last season and 14th in offensive EPA with two significant offseason moves. The Broncos traded for wide receiver Jaylen Waddle , and Payton relinquished primary playcalling duties to newly promoted offensive coordinator Davis Webb. But when the stakes are high, the Broncos are confident they'll prevail. Or, as cornerback Riley Moss phrases it, they'll "just be hard to kill.'' That mindset helped the 2015 Broncos win the franchise's third Super Bowl. And Talib hopes that these Broncos can turn all that accountability, talent and big-moment success into their own Super Bowl rings. "Of course we all want success, but you can't gatekeep s---, don't gatekeep information, don't keep secrets," Talib said. "We kept it right with each other, everybody's success is the real success. "They play good ball, so you know they have the people who keep it right."

Arizona Cardinals 2d ESPN staff NFL win rate metrics leaderboard: Ranking the best in pass rushing, run stopping and blocking 2d ESPN Analytics Michael DiRocco Sep 14, 2026, 06:00 AM ET Close Michael DiRocco is an NFL Nation reporter at ESPN and covers the Jacksonville Jaguars. He previously covered the University of Florida for over a decade for ESPN and the Florida Times-Union. DiRocco graduated from Jacksonville University and is a multiple APSE award winner. Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- Trevor Lawrence has not been his best in September. Statistically, anyway. The Jacksonville Jaguars ' quarterback has won only 33% of games, completed only 60% of his passes, and posted a Total QBR of 47 in September -- all the worst marks of any month of his career. But on Sunday, he had one of the best days of his career in a 34-10 rout of the Cleveland Browns at EverBank Stadium. He looked a lot like the quarterback who got on a roll in the second half of 2025, when he led the Jaguars to the playoffs and earned MVP consideration. That version of Lawrence will need to continue if the Jaguars are going to successfully manage a five-game stretch that includes four 2025 playoff teams. "When he is playing to the best of his ability like we know he can, the offense starts clicking and he makes some big plays downfield with some great throws, and we feed off of that," running back Bhayshul Tuten said. "We love him." The sixth-year QB was on a roll against the Browns. He completed 78.3% of his passes for 245 yards and four touchdowns with a 93.4 Total QBR. It was just the third time in his career that he has thrown four or more TD passes. On passes of 10-plus air yards, Lawrence completed 10 of 11 attempts for 179 yards and a career-high three touchdowns, per NFL Next Gen Stats. Spreading the ball worked really well for the offense. Lawrence completed passes to nine players, and each TD pass went to a different player. "I thought he spread the ball around, trusted the guys that were in to make plays," head coach Liam Coen said. "I thought we protected him really well, thought we mixed it up from the run game and some different things to keep them off-balance to allow Trevor to continue to do what he does. He did some really good stuff off-schedule again today, especially the touchdown to Jakobi [Meyers] , I thought was a phenomenal throw and play in the back of the end zone. "So was definitely pleased with the way that Trevor ran the offense today." It was the sixth time in the past nine regular-season games (all victories) that the Jaguars have scored 30-plus points. Lawrence has 23 touchdown passes -- more than any other quarterback -- and only five interceptions in those nine games. But the Jaguars will need him to continue that pace for the next five weeks if they are going to establish themselves as legitimate AFC contenders. That starts with Sunday's game at the Denver Broncos , followed by a home game against the New England Patriots , a road game versus the Cincinnati Bengals and then back-to-back games in London against the Philadelphia Eagles and Houston Texans . "I feel really comfortable, really confident in what we're doing," Lawrence said. "I think last year at this time, I knew what we were doing, but it was still -- you're still getting used to the game plan and the moving parts of the offense, which was a lot, which is a big change for me. I think there was that dynamic of still trying to get completely comfortable in it. "It was awesome to get a win in Week 1 but excited now. We have a big challenge next week and got to turn the page and go put together another great game plan." Lawrence's best game of 2025 came against the Broncos in Denver. He withstood a strong pass rush -- five sacks and 14 QB hits -- and threw for 279 yards and three touchdowns with no turnovers in a 34-20 victory. The Jaguars didn't start that game fast but pulled away with two third-quarter touchdowns. Lawrence would like the Jaguars to repeat what they did against the Browns, scoring two first-quarter touchdowns and leading 24-0 at the half. "You want to start the game fast and play well in that first possession so you can settle in as soon as possible and not give the ball back to the other team," he said. "I think that's always something you want to do, but I think it comes down to preparation. Also, every game is different. You don't know exactly what the defense is going to do first series, and so there's a lot of moving parts. "For us to start fast today like we did, that's the goal moving forward, obviously, and going to continue to build on that." Which could make this Lawrence's best September.

Raanan joined ESPN in 2016. Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. -- John Harbaugh's first game as New York Giants coach went as planned. His team played physical football during a 28-20 win over the rival Dallas Cowboys on Sunday night at MetLife Stadium. It left the longtime head coach, who spent the previous 18 seasons with the Baltimore Ravens , pleased with his Big Apple debut. "This was really special because these guys, these players, these guys who have believed from the beginning, they don't bat an eye," Harbaugh said after watching his team outplay the opposition. "They just try to do the right thing every single day. They try to be on point. And even when they're not on point, they're going to bounce back and make it right. Maybe there is a mistake. Maybe there is a false start. They find a way to make a play and erase the mistake and make it right and make it better. "Buying into that kind of mindset, just when you see it in practice and see it happen in a game, that is what as a coach you feel so good about." Harbaugh came to New York wanting to build a big, physical team. The Giants outrushed Dallas 165 yards to 69. He wanted his team to play disciplined situational football. New York ran out the final 5:16 of the contest to preserve the win. Afterward, Harbaugh was presented a game ball from team owner John Mara. "We have one more game ball. It's his first victory as New York Giants head coach," Mara said before handing it to Harbaugh. Harbaugh's players proceeded to shower him with cheers. They jumped and danced around him. Harbaugh did the same. He later celebrated in the locker room with his parents, who came in Friday to witness their younger son's first game as Giants coach. Harbaugh, who won a Super Bowl with the Ravens, was asked in his postgame news conference to rank Sunday's game among his 205 career victories. "It's No. 1," he said. "Because it's the one right now." This is something he learned from his dad, Jack, a former longtime coach at Western Kentucky . Jack always told his son the most recent win was the best win. "'John, you never had a better win than that,'" he recalled hearing from his dad on every car ride home. "He says it every time. I think this time it might be true." His players took pride in getting Harbaugh his first Giants win. They've embraced their new coach and what he has preached. It helps that the blueprint Harbaugh laid out when he first arrived worked to perfection in his first game. "From day one, he told us he wants to punish the other team and run the ball and throw play-action passes. That's what we did [Sunday night]," said running back Cam Skattebo , who led the Giants with 81 yards rushing. "The stuff we did worked. They trusted the plan, and we came out here and executed." So, the Harbaugh era got off to a good start. The Giants started the season with a win for just the second time in 10 years. It was a statement against a Dallas team that had beaten the Giants in 16 of the past 18 matchups and perhaps was a warning to the NFC East that they could be a threat with a Super Bowl-winning coach now at the helm. "It was huge," New York quarterback Jaxson Dart said. "I just think that we have so much respect for Coach [Harbaugh], and this team will do whatever he says because we have all the faith that he's going to put us in the best situation. The identity of a team starts at the top. It starts with how he's conducted himself, with how he's created a tough team. "We want to take that on our shoulders, and we bought in to what his plan is week in and week out. We're definitely happy to get it for him. We're just really happy we did it, not only for the players but for the organization."

Arizona Cardinals 2d ESPN staff NFL win rate metrics leaderboard: Ranking the best in pass rushing, run stopping and blocking 2d ESPN Analytics Todd Archer Sep 14, 2026, 01:31 AM ET Close Todd Archer is an NFL reporter at ESPN and covers the Dallas Cowboys. Archer has covered the NFL since 1997 and Dallas since 2003. He joined ESPN in 2010. Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. -- Off the top of his head, Dallas Cowboys coach Brian Schottenheimer, who has spent most of his life around the NFL, could not recall a more disappointing season-opening defeat, but Sunday's 28-20 loss to the New York Giants was up there. "Been around a long time so maybe, but right now, this one feels pretty bad just because at the end of the day, we just didn't perform the way we're capable of playing," Schottenheimer said. "We didn't play defense the way we're capable of playing. We didn't play offense in the first half the way we're capable of playing. ... But we're not going to panic. This is a long season, and we know we're not going to go undefeated. That's real, but that's not the biggest issue we have." A rebuilt Cowboys defense could not slow down the Giants' offense. New York converted 9 of 11 third-down chances, and one of the two that was missed occurred on a kneel-down to close out the game. After quarterback Dak Prescott nicknamed the Cowboys' offense the "Greatest Offense There Is" in training camp, the unit started slowly and had the ball just twice in the second half. Despite missing the playoffs each of the past two seasons, the Cowboys entered 2026 optimistic that things would be different but opened the year with a divisional loss just as they did in 2025, when they lost to the Philadelphia Eagles . For the second straight season, the Cowboys play another NFC East foe in Week 2 when the Washington Commanders visit AT&T Stadium. Last year, the Cowboys beat the Giants 40-37 in Game 2 of the season, a sign that Dallas' defense would struggle and the offense could put up points to finish 7-9-1. "I know the way that we approach things, I know that our routine, I know that our standard, I know that the way that we practice is the right way," Prescott said. "So, my message is echoing: don't change, don't flinch, don't blink. This is a long year." The Cowboys had just seven possessions, and one came with 20 seconds left in the first half after the Giants turned Prescott's interception into a go-ahead touchdown pass from Jaxson Dart to tight end Isaiah Likely . A defense that featured eight new starters from Week 1 in 2025 suffered communication breakdowns. Likely broke free in the end zone after linebacker Dee Winters and cornerback DaRon Bland jumped an underneath receiver. Prescott said he tried to throw the pass away after he was flushed from the pocket while under duress, but safety Jevon Holland made a sliding interception. "That was a huge part in the game," Prescott said. "They scored before half. They got the ball to start the [second] half, and they went and scored, limited our possessions in the second half, only gave us two possessions, and that was the game right there." The Giants' offense was on the field for 21 minutes, 33 seconds in the second half. New York finished with 165 yards rushing on 37 carries. Dart became the fifth quarterback with at least three touchdown passes and 50 yards rushing in a team's season opener in NFL history. The Cowboys lost veteran safety Malik Hooker , who suffered a fractured forearm in the fourth quarter. "We've got to definitely look in the mirrors, especially as a defense and go this week and do it," defensive tackle Quinnen Williams said. "We've got the guys in this defensive room. This defensive unit is really good. We've got the guys to be accountable and get better." Prescott completed 22 of 34 attempts for just 175 yards. He has now lost two straight starts against the Giants after winning 14 in a row. The Cowboys, who had the fewest three-and-outs in 2025, opened Sunday with a three-and-out. Dallas failed to generate a play of more than 17 yards all game, and George Pickens and CeeDee Lamb had opportunities go through their hands. Last year, the Cowboys had at least two 20-yard receptions in every game and finished with 56 as a team. Lamb and Pickens combined for 38 of them. But the Cowboys ran just 52 offensive plays Sunday. "It's just more so when we do get our opportunities, we do got to make the most of it," Lamb said. "It doesn't matter how many opps we get." Twice, the Cowboys came within one score in the second half, and the second time they had a potential 2-point opportunity wiped out because of a taunting penalty on running back Javonte Williams as he pointed the ball at a Giants defender while crossing the goal line with 5:21 to play. The 15-yard penalty forced the Cowboys to kick an extra point, and Brandon Aubrey 's 48-yard kick was wide right. It was the eighth penalty of a nine-penalty performance from the Cowboys. Schottenheimer called Williams one of the Cowboys' "most dependable players." "We're getting ready to try to go in for two and make it a one-score game," Schottenheimer said. "We're going for the win. That's not like Javonte." The Cowboys didn't get the ball back, with Dart kneeling it three straight times to seal the win. "This is a humbling business, and we got humbled tonight, and that's what I told the guys," Schottenheimer said. "We lost Mile 1 of a 17-mile marathon, and we have to be better. We will be better. The only way to do that is get back to work."

Arizona Cardinals 2d ESPN staff NFL win rate metrics leaderboard: Ranking the best in pass rushing, run stopping and blocking 2d ESPN Analytics NFL Nation Sep 13, 2026, 11:50 PM ET Close NFL Nation is made up of 32 team-specific reporters who cover the NFL year-round across ESPN.com, ESPN television shows, ESPN Radio, ESPN+ and social media platforms. It was established ahead of the 2013 season. Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions The 2026 NFL season is already off to an exciting start. In the early window Sunday, the Bears and Panthers combined for 96 points, the most in a season opener in NFL history, per ESPN Research. The host Jaguars easily handled the Browns in quarterback Deshaun Watson 's first regular-season game since October 2024. The Bills looked sharp offensively in Joe Brady's head coaching debut against the Texans, and the Lions needed overtime to get past the Saints. In the late window, the Cardinals and Raiders won in the respective debuts of first-year coaches Mike LaFleur and Klint Kubiak. The Commanders fell despite a comeback against division foe Philadelphia. And after losing quarterback Kyler Murray to a concussion early, the Vikings scored 29 unanswered to defeat the Packers. The Giants finished things off by beating the Cowboys on Sunday night, marking the first time since 2009 both New York teams opened with a victory. Our NFL Nation reporters reacted to all the action, answering lingering questions coming out of each game and detailing everything else you need to know for teams that played Sunday. Fantasy football analysts Matt Bowen and Tristan Cockcroft also have fantasy takeaways from each matchup. Let's get to it. Jump to: DAL-NYG | GB-MIN | WSH-PHI MIA-LV | ARI-LAC | CHI-CAR BUF-HOU | NO-DET | BAL-IND ATL-PIT | NYJ-TEN | TB-CIN CLE-JAX Catch up on weekday games: SF-LAR | NE-SEA N.Y. Giants 28, Dallas 20 Catch up on the action: Box score | Recap Giants Should the Giants be taken seriously in the NFC East? This was a statement game for the John Harbaugh Giants. They looked like the better team in beating a Cowboys squad that had prevailed in 16 of its previous 18 meetings with the Giants. New York's offense looked dangerous with a power running game (165 yards) led by Cam Skattebo (18 carries, 81 yards), and quarterback Jaxson Dart was in command throughout. The defense also looked greatly improved. With neither the Eagles nor Commanders looking dominant in Week1, the Giants could be a real threat in the NFC East. For the first time in years, it's not an outlandish thought. What to make of the QB performance: Brilliant. Dart was in control throughout, running and throwing with precision. He finished 23-of-29 for 230 passing yards with three touchdown and added 54 rushing yards. The chemistry that Dart showed all summer with new tight end Isaiah Likely translated to the opener. Likely caught eight passes on eight targets for 78 yards with two touchdowns and helped ice the game late with two big third-down receptions. -- Jordan Raanan Next game: at Rams (Monday, Sept. 21, 8:15 p.m. ET) Cowboys Will this serve as a wake-up call for the Cowboys? After a drama-free offseason, the return of a top-tier offense and a revamped defense, expectations were high. Though there are 16 more games to go, the loss to the Giants showed the Cowboys have a lot of work to do. An ill-timed Dak Prescott interception at the end of the first half led to a Giants' TD. There were far too many penalties in the first half (seven, tied for the most in an opener since 2008) and a costly one in the fourth quarter, as Javonte Williams ' taunting penalty led to a missed extra point attempt in a one-score game. The Giants were able to control the line of scrimmage and the clock in the second half to win a game that went according to the Giants' desired script. Most surprising performance: Things were supposed to be different for this Cowboys defense. Not necessarily a massive move to the top of the league, but they were disappointing throughout Christian Parker's first game as playcaller. The end-of-half work that saw New York go ahead 14-7 was filled with coverage breakdowns. The second half opened with the Cowboys needing to call timeout because they had only 10 defenders on the field, and they could not come up with any stops in the final two quarters. With eight new starters from last season's opener and another handful of new key contributors, it's clear it will take time for it to come together. -- Todd Archer Next game: vs. Commanders (Sunday, 4:25 p.m. ET) Fantasy football takeaway: Likely paced the Giants with eight catches -- the most by any Giants tight end in nearly three years -- with two going for touchdowns. His 27.8 fantasy points led the position, and are an indicator he'll be involved enough to be a weekly TE1. -- Cockcroft Minnesota 39, Green Bay 22 Catch up on the action: Box score | Recap Vikings What now at quarterback? For the second consecutive season, and for the third campaign in the past four, the Vikings are dealing with an injury to their quarterback. This time, new starter Kyler Murray made it only 11 plays -- and they were 11 shaky plays, at that -- before suffering a concussion at the end of a first-quarter scramble. Backup Carson Wentz , named the No. 2 quarterback last week after he was a bystander in the competition between Murray and J.J. McCarthy this summer, was understandably rusty at the outset but hung in to throw three touchdown passes and avoid a turnover. Wentz will be the starter until Murray is cleared to return. Trend to watch: The Vikings blitzed Packers quarterback Jordan Love on nearly every first-half snap (15-of-18, or 83%), and Love burned them repeatedly en route to putting up 19 points. Defensive coordinator Brian Flores adjusted with more variety in the second half, taking down the blitz rate to 63%. It wasn't the only reason the Packers struggled to score thereafter, but it made the blitzes the Vikings did execute more effective. -- Kevin Seifert Next game: at Bears (Sunday, 1 p.m. ET) Packers Did the Packers learn nothing from last year? So much for all that offseason talk about finishing. Week 1 followed the same script from late last season: Grab the lead, make major mistakes in the second half and let the opponent back in the game. The blunders were many in this matchup: a special teams miscue (allowing a 69-yard kickoff return); a blown coverage (leaving tight end T.J. Hockenson wide open for a touchdown); bad penalties (three of them on the Vikings' go-ahead drive that wiped out a pair of would-have-been third-down stops and nullified an interception); shoddy offensive line play; and a poor coaching decision (opting to take a field goal off the board on a penalty then failing on the ensuing QB sneak). What to make of the QB performance: Love, despite a 387-yard passing game, barely had a chance, especially down the stretch, thanks to a disastrous performance by his offensive line. Being without starting left guard Aaron Banks (knee) wasn't the reason the Vikings recorded 15 QB hits on Love; it was because the Packers couldn't handle the myriad of blitzes. When the Packers needed a fourth-quarter drive to regain the lead, Love was sacked on back-to-back plays, losing a fumble on the second one that was returned to Green Bay's 1-yard line. -- Rob Demovsky Next game: at Jets (Sunday, 1 p.m. ET) Fantasy football takeaway: Christian Watson 's 32.7 fantasy points were the second most among wide receivers in Week 1 through the late window. He caught 6-of-8 targets for 147 yards and two touchdowns for the Pack. With an expanding route tree and big-play speed, Watson can be safely played as a lower-tier WR2 for Week 2. -- Bowen Philadelphia 24, Washington 22 Catch up on the action: Box score | Recap Eagles Did the Eagles' new offense pass the test Week 1? There was a boom-or-bust element to it, but the explosive plays carried them to a passing grade and a win over Washington. From WR Dontayvion Wicks ' 64-yard reception (a career high) to QB Jalen Hurts ' 22-yard scramble on third-and-18 to TE Dallas Goedert 's 43-yard score moments later, there was plenty to be encouraged about from offensive coordinator Sean Mannion's debut. Some issues along the offensive front (left guard Landon Dickerson looked as if he was laboring) and long stretches of ineffectiveness brought back memories of 2025, but patience is required while Philly breaks in a new system. What to make of the QB performance: Hurts threw three touchdowns, was timely with his runs and didn't commit a turnover. The pass-and-catch between the signal-caller and new WR1 DeVonta Smith along the right sideline late in the third quarter was a thing of beauty. Hurts was at his best when attacking downfield, completing 6 of 9 such attempts for 176 yards. -- Tim McManus Next game: at Titans (Sunday, 1 p.m. ET) Commanders Did quarterback Jayden Daniels show enough to inspire a bounce-back season? Daniels looked sharp this summer in new coordinator David Blough's offense. But for most of Sunday's game -- his first since Week 14 last season -- the offense struggled against one of the NFL's best defenses. Daniels hesitated too many times because he didn't have an open target or wasn't confident in what he saw. That's concerning, as one of his best traits is being decisive. In the first half, he completed 6 of 16 passes for 43 yards. Daniels still finished strong, leading two scoring drives to nearly tie the score. But if Washington is going to avoid a bad start, Blough and Daniels need to find a better rhythm early. Most surprising performance: Wide receiver Terry McLaurin did not catch a pass until less than five minutes remained in the contest. He finished with just two catches and four targets. It's not what Blough had in mind when he took over, saying he wanted to get McLaurin 10 targets per game. But the Eagles often doubled him, rolled coverage his way or simply blanketed him. Best quote from the locker room: Philadelphia had four plays of 31 yards or longer that accounted for 180 of its 318 total yards, which frustrated Washington rookie LB Sonny Styles . "Those four explosives determined the game. Aside from those plays, we played pretty well. But when you put those chunk [plays] on the table, it's hard to win the game," Styles said. - - John Keim Next game: at Cowboys (Sunday, 4:25 p.m. ET) Fantasy football takeaway: Wicks caught just two of four targets this week, but he finished with 77 yards and a touchdown (15.3 fantasy points). He has the ability to uncover over the top, and he scored on an end zone throw from Hurts. Rostered in just 10.1% of ESPN leagues, I would add Wicks this week as a bench stash. -- Bowen Las Vegas 27, Miami 13 Catch up on the action: Box score | Recap Raiders Is the offensive line's performance sustainable? Yes. It's just one game, but the Raiders showed that a new coaching staff and scheme have paid dividends for the O-line. Running back Ashton Jeanty was the star, but that wouldn't have been the case without a strong performance from the players in the trenches. It will be intriguing to see if the line can translate this performance against tougher competition in the coming weeks. Two positions to monitor are left guard and right tackle. Left guard Spencer Burford gave up a team-high four pressures. Right tackle DJ Glaze allowed only one pressure on 31 pass-block snaps, which was a good sign after he struggled in 2025. Trend to watch: Edge rusher Maxx Crosby could be on a pitch count. During the Dolphins' third drive, Crosby sat out six consecutive plays. At the league meeting in March, Las Vegas general manager John Spytek hinted at the possibility of monitoring Crosby's snap count after he underwent offseason knee surgery. Crosby totaled 1.5 sacks and seven pressures against Miami. If managing his snap count can improve Crosby's longevity, then it's a smart decision. Kwity Paye might be the one who steps up; he had two sacks and five pressures Sunday. -- Ryan McFadden Next game: at Chargers (Sunday, 4:05 p.m. ET) Dolphins How concerning is the Dolphins' offensive performance? No Miami player besides Caleb Douglas consistently got open. Game script impacted the Dolphins' ability to call run plays, but even when they rushed, ball carrier De'Von Achane was stuffed on nearly 20% of his attempts. Quarterback Malik Willis was pressured 17 times and sacked five times. Considering the Dolphins' lack of experience at wide receiver, it's fairly easy to write this off as growing pains. But the schedule doesn't get easier, and Miami's offense next gets a 49ers defense that shut down the Rams in Week 1. What to make of the QB performance: Willis was steady, albeit unspectacular in the first half, as Miami's receivers struggled to get open downfield. Willis appeared to press a bit in the second half, highlighted by a head-scratching interception that looked more like an arm punt on second down from deep in his own territory. Willis showed a willingness to make plays with his legs, but this was a relatively uninspiring performance against what could end up being one of the Dolphins' easier matchups this season. -- Marcel Louis-Jacques Next game: at 49ers (Sunday, 4:25 p.m. ET) Fantasy football takeaway: The ankle injury Jeanty suffered during the preseason no longer appears to be an issue. The second-year running back scored 32.7 fantasy points, thanks in part to a pair of 13-yard receiving touchdowns. Sure, the matchup helped, but this performance reaffirmed his fantasy RB1 status. -- Cockcroft Arizona 26, L.A. Chargers 14 Catch up on the action: Box score | Recap Cardinals What does an impressive upset win say about Mike LaFleur's impact on the Cardinals? Sunday certainly looked like a new dawn for Arizona under the first-year coach. It wasn't perfect, by any stretch. But the Cardinals' upset win -- they were 8.5-point underdogs on DraftKings -- showcased LaFleur's offense and all of its weapons, as Arizona moved efficiently and swiftly downfield all afternoon. Add in a few key plays by the defense at opportune times -- including a forced and recovered fumble and a blocked kick that set up a touchdown -- and suddenly a team that lost its final nine outings in 2025 looks confident for future games. What to make of the QB performance: Jacoby Brissett played as well as anyone could've hoped in his first game in a new offense without the benefit of working through the nuances of it during OTAs or minicamp. The quarterback had one hiccup but otherwise turned in a clean and efficient performance with 277 passing yards and a touchdown on 27-for-37 passing. -- Josh Weinfuss Next game: vs. Seahawks (Sunday, 4:25 p.m. ET) Chargers Is there reason for concern about Mike McDaniel's offense? Much has been made about how explosive the pairing between quarterback Justin Herbert and McDaniel might be this season, and the O-coordinator hasn't shied away from that, saying he anticipated his receivers would have career highs across the board. On Sunday, those expectations seemed farfetched. It was the Cardinals' offense, however, that had the explosiveness with 393 total yards, as compared with L.A.'s 268. The hope for the Chargers is that they just need time to make this major offensive shift under McDaniel. Stat to know: Coach Jim Harbaugh has gone for it on fourth down inside the 20-yard line just seven times with the Chargers, converting three. This makes Harbaugh's decision Sunday all the more surprising. With just under two minutes remaining in the second quarter and the Chargers down 10-7, Harbaugh went go for it on fourth from the 3-yard line. Defensive tackle Dante Stills sacked Herbert, and the Cardinals went on to sink a field goal to extend their lead to six points before halftime. The Chargers' 38 fourth-down attempts under Harbaugh since 2024 are tied for third fewest by any team, per ESPN Research. -- Kris Rhim Next game: vs. Raiders (Sunday, 4:05 p.m. ET) Fantasy football takeaway: Brissett kept the Cards' offense afloat and most notably helped tight end Trey McBride reach his eighth game of 20-plus fantasy points in their past 13 starts working together. They'll need this level of chemistry to survive one of the league's toughest schedules in 2026. -- Cockcroft Chicago 59, Carolina 37 Catch up on the action: Box score | Recap Bears Can the Bears' offense be expected to overcome defensive woes all season? Their 59 points were the fourth most in franchise history. Coach Ben Johnson's goal was to have the highest-scoring offense ever and to score every time the unit touches the field; not a bad start with that goal. Chicago's 552 yards were their third most in a game in the Super Bowl era. There's plenty to clean up, from penalties to TE Colston Loveland 's usage, but Caleb Williams ' playmaking and a rushing attack that scored a franchise-record six TDs proved decisive. The Bears' defense, though, will need to get healthy and improve for the team to reach its overall goals. What to make of the QB performance: Williams (21-for-29, 269 yards, two TDs, 124.1 rating) proved again his legs are legit difference makers. He recorded his first career game with multiple rushing touchdowns and was prolific when he escaped the pocket to make throws. He rushed for 65 yards on 10 carries. -- Courtney Cronin Next game: vs. Vikings (Sunday, 1 p.m. ET) Panthers How much stock can Panthers put into an historically bad defensive performance? After spending a fortune on outside linebacker Jaelan Phillips and inside linebacker Devin Lloyd in free agency, the Panthers expected their defense to be greatly improved. However, the unit was completely dismantled in an all-time horrible outing. The Panthers gave up 442 net yards and seven scoring drives before the end of the third quarter. And the 59 points scored by the Bears were the most allowed by the Panthers in franchise history. Defensive coordinator Ejiro Evero frequently came under fire during the previous three seasons. And Sunday's performance was easily his worst to date. What to make of the QB performance: With the defense faltering all afternoon, Bryce Young did his best to keep his squad even in the opener. With offensive coordinator Brad Idzik calling plays for the first time, Young dwarfed his three previous Week 1 performances with 361 passing yards, four total touchdowns and an interception. He led six scoring drives in a shootout that Carolina ultimately lost largely because of the defense. -- Mike Kaye Next game: at Falcons (Sunday, 1 p.m. ET) Fantasy football takeaway: Williams led all quarterbacks in the early window with 37.26 fantasy points. Yes, Williams showed his rare playmaking ability as a runner, but his efficiency from the pocket was on full display as he completed 72.4% of his passes. He'll be a top-five QB in my ranks for Week 2. -- Bowen Buffalo 36, Houston 31 Catch up on the action: Box score | Recap Bills Is this the version of the Bills' offense we should expect with former coordinator Joe Brady now in charge? We were promised more aggressiveness and downfield attacking, which we sure got a peek at Sunday. Of his 11 passes in the first half, quarterback Josh Allen went 6-of-7 for 149 yards and a touchdown on throws that traveled more than 10 air yards downfield, according to ESPN research. He had 11 completions of more than 10 air yards, tied for his most in a game in his career. Stat to know: This was Allen's ninth career game with two passing touchdowns and two rushing touchdowns. That's five more than any other player in NFL history. Steve Young had four. Allen also became the first player in NFL history to reach 300 combined touchdowns in his first nine seasons. -- Judy Battista Next game: vs. Lions (Thursday, 8:15 p.m. ET) Texans How did the Texans' defense struggle so badly? It has been awhile since Houston's starting defense has allowed 30 points. The last time the unit gave up 30 in a game in which the starters finished was Christmas Day 2024 against the Ravens. Today, the offense gave them 31 points -- and usually that's more than enough for a Texans' win under coach DeMeco Ryans. A silver lining is the unit allowed only 12 points in the second half after giving up 24 in the first. But still, 36 points is unacceptable for a defense that believes it's the best. Most surprising performance: Running back David Montgomery was viewed as a strong trade acquisition by the team, but kicking off his Texans career with three scrimmage touchdowns was impressive. Two of those came on the ground and one through the air for a total of 79 yards. It was the second game of his career with three scrimmage TDs. -- DJ Bien-Aime Next game: vs. Bengals (Sunday, 1 p.m. ET) Fantasy football takeaway: Montgomery (28.9 points) didn't have a very efficient day running the ball (3.0 yards per carry), but the red zone usage gives him a boost. He scored twice on red zone carries (one on the goal line), and he was targeted on a schemed throw from Stroud to find the end zone. Montgomery remains a touchdown-dependent RB2 in Week 2. -- Bowen Detroit 31, New Orleans 30 (OT) Catch up on the action: Box score | Recap Lions Should the Lions be worried about the defense, or is this what we should expect? Honestly, it might be somewhere in between, as the Saints' offense likely won't be this stellar throughout the season. When Detroit's offense struggled in the first half, the defense held the Saints scoreless and created three turnovers. But then it gave up 24 points in the second half. Edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson finished with two sacks, while S Chuck Clark and LB Derrick Barnes both snagged interceptions, but the defense was still susceptible to explosive plays. That was the same issue last year. Perhaps the eventual return of safeties Kerby Joseph (knee) and Brian Branch (Achilles) from IR will help. Stat to know: Jahmyr Gibbs ' second TD marked his 51st score in 50 career games, making him the sixth player in NFL history to reach at least 50 touchdowns in 50 or fewer games, per ESPN Research. Chuck Foreman (44 games), Steve Van Buren (45), Jim Brown (46), Larry Johnson (48) and Marcus Allen (49) round out the list. Best quote from the locker room: Lions QB Jared Goff on tough overtime win: "I don't care how it happens. If we're up and they come back or we're down and we come back, it doesn't matter ... Yeah, of course, we'd love to keep scoring and win 49-0 of course, I'm not saying that. But listen, it's the NFL. This thing's hard. Week 1's very hard and we're happy to get a win." -- Eric Woodyard Next game: at Bills (Thursday, 8:15 p.m. ET) Saints What will we see from the Saints' offense next week after its slow start? It's hard to know whether the slow start in Detroit was a result of simple season-opening jitters or a true concern moving forward. The Saints took a long time to finally look right on offense. The offense came up big late and was a two-point conversion away from winning in OT, but it had too much to overcome because of its first-half struggles. What to make of the QB performance: It was a tale of two Shoughs. He looked out of sync with the offense and had several turnovers that put the Saints in a 21-0 hole by the third quarter. But he was able to generate a lot of momentum, nearly winning the game in overtime while becoming the first Saints QB to pass for 400 yards since Drew Brees in 2018. Best quote from the locker room: Wide receiver Chris Olave , who had a personal best 182 yards, said he was happy to be wearing a Guardian cap after he took a hard hit in practice earlier in the offseason. "Y'all know all the head injuries I done had in my career. It was just a decision I had made. I got kids now. I want to be able to live the long game. It's not all about football. I want to live regular life after I'm done with football. I love my kids to death. I don't really care how it looks no more. I just got to throw it on and shoot, it did me good today." -- Katherine Terrell Next game: at Ravens (Sunday, 1 p.m. ET) Fantasy football takeaway: Shough certainly seemed to have the skills as a passer to help fantasy managers sooner rather than later in standard 10-team formats. Coming back from two touchdowns behind, he scored nearly the entirety of his 23.2 fantasy points on the Saints' final five drives. -- Cockcroft Baltimore 41, Indianapolis 23 Catch up on the action: Box score | Recap Ravens What are the Ravens going to do at wide receiver if Zay Flowers misses any time? The Ravens may need to add a veteran receiver depending on the severity of Flowers' injury. Flowers was on his way to a career day (150 yards and one touchdown) before aggravating a left hamstring injury late in the first half, which forced him to sit out the entire second half. Flowers' injury is compounded by the loss of promising rookie Ja'Kobi Lane , who didn't play in the second half because of a wrist injury. That leaves Baltimore without its No. 1 (Flowers) and No. 3 receivers (Lane). The Ravens' only healthy wide receivers are: Rashod Bateman , LaJohntay Wester , who is primarily a punt returner, Chris Moore , who was elevated from the practice squad, and Elijah Sarratt , a rookie fourth-round pick who was a healthy scratch. Before Flowers' injury, quarterback Lamar Jackson was 10-of-13 for 214 yards and a touchdown. Without Flowers, Jackson was 7-of-12 for 110 yards. It was Henry's 26th game with more than 100 yards rushing and multiple touchdowns, which moved him past Jim Brown for the most in NFL history.
